questions.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
o: 1 Ω
2 Ω
9 Ω
questions.why: Parallel: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. The result is always below the smallest branch. In series you would add them (9 Ω).

questions.q: A 0.02 Ω busbar joint carries 500 A. How much heat does it dissipate?
o: 5 kW
250 kW
questions.why: P = I²R = 500² × 0.02 = 5,000 W. Heating grows with the square of current, which is why loose joints at high current are a fire risk.

questions.q: A DC bus at 800 V carries 100 A. What is the power?
o: 8 kW
80 kW
800 kW
8 MW

questions.q: A battery delivers 2 MW for 3 hours. How much energy is that?
o: 0.67 MWh
1.5 MWh
5 MWh
6 MWh
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 2 MW × 3 h = 6 MWh. MW is a rate, MWh is an amount.

questions.q: Why does a higher DC bus voltage reduce cable losses for the same power?
o: Copper resistance falls as the operating voltage rises
Current falls at fixed power, and the loss scales with I²
The voltage drop along the cable turns negative at high voltage
Skin effect disappears once the bus voltage is high enough
questions.why: For fixed P = VI, doubling V halves I, and I²R loss falls to a quarter. This is a main reason utility-scale systems moved to 1,500 V DC.

questions.q: A cable has 0.1 Ω total resistance and carries 200 A for one hour. How much energy is lost as heat?
o: 0.2 kWh
2 kWh
4 kWh
20 kWh
questions.why: P = I²R = 200² × 0.1 = 4,000 W. Over one hour that is 4 kWh.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a fuse or DC breaker rated with a breaking (interrupting) capacity?
o: Open safely at the maximum fault current
Hold the normal load current continuously
Balance charge between cells in a string
Smooth ripple voltage on the DC bus
questions.why: A protective device must open the circuit at the highest fault current the source can deliver. Batteries have very low impedance, so DC fault currents can be enormous.

questions.q: A load draws 1,000 kVA at power factor 0.8. What is the real power?
o: 200 kW
800 kW
questions.why: P = S × PF = 1,000 × 0.8 = 800 kW. The rest of the apparent power is reactive (600 kvar).

questions.q: In a balanced three-phase star (wye) connection, how are line-to-line and phase voltage related?
o: Line voltage equals phase voltage
Line voltage is √3 times phase voltage
Line voltage is phase voltage divided by √3
Line voltage is three times phase voltage
questions.why: In a star connection the line-to-line voltage is √3 times the line-to-neutral voltage, for example 400 V line-to-line from 230 V phase.

questions.q: A converter injects reactive power into a weak grid. What is the typical effect on the local voltage?
o: Voltage at the connection point rises
Voltage at the connection point falls
Voltage stays unchanged
Grid frequency rises noticeably
questions.why: Injecting reactive power (capacitive behaviour) raises voltage at the point of connection, and more strongly where the grid is weak (low short-circuit ratio).

questions.q: Which quantity is measured in kvar?
o: Real power
Reactive power
Energy
Apparent energy loss
questions.why: kvar measures reactive power, which oscillates between source and load without doing net work. Real power is kW, apparent power is kVA.

questions.q: What does a low short-circuit ratio (SCR) at a connection point tell you?
o: Weak grid: voltage reacts strongly to power changes
Strong grid: voltage stays steady under load swings
Battery undersized for the site rating
Harmonic distortion will stay low at the point
questions.why: SCR compares grid short-circuit power with the plant rating. A low value means a weak grid: voltage moves a lot when power or reactive power changes, and control stability becomes harder.

questions.q: A 100 Ah cell is discharged at 50 A. What is the C-rate?
o: 1C
2C
5C
questions.why: C-rate = current / capacity = 50 / 100 = 0.5C, so a full discharge takes about 2 hours.

questions.q: A pack has 16 cells in series, each 3.2 V nominal and 280 Ah, with 2 such strings in parallel (16S2P). What are the pack voltage and capacity?
questions.why: Series adds voltage: 16 × 3.2 = 51.2 V. Parallel adds capacity: 2 × 280 = 560 Ah. Energy is about 28.7 kWh.

questions.q: Why is LFP often preferred over NMC for stationary storage?
o: Its energy density is much higher, so containers are smaller
Its structure is more thermally stable and lasts more cycles
Its nominal voltage is higher, which cuts cable cost
It has almost zero self-discharge compared with NMC
questions.why: LFP has lower energy density, but its olivine structure is more stable (higher thermal runaway onset) and it lasts more cycles. In stationary sites, safety and cost per cycle matter more than weight.

questions.q: What does state of health (SOH) usually express?
o: Present capacity or resistance versus new
Energy discharged divided by energy charged
Charge left as a percent of usable capacity
Cell temperature versus its permitted limit
questions.why: SOH tracks degradation, commonly as capacity relative to nameplate, and sometimes as resistance growth. State of charge (SOC) is the fill level.

questions.q: What does round-trip efficiency measure for a battery system?
o: Capacity today over capacity at commissioning
Voltage at end of discharge divided by start voltage
Energy out divided by energy in over a full cycle
Cycles completed per year over cycles warranted
questions.why: Round-trip efficiency = discharged energy / charged energy (AC to AC for the whole system). Losses come from cells, PCS, transformer, and auxiliaries such as cooling.

questions.q: Why does available capacity fall at low temperature?
o: Series strings stop sharing the current evenly
Ion diffusion slows and resistance rises
Cell chemistry changes permanently each winter
Electrolyte expands and leaks from the cells
questions.why: Cold slows lithium-ion transport and charge-transfer kinetics, so internal resistance rises and usable capacity and power drop. Charging at low temperature also risks lithium plating.

questions.q: What is the difference between a cell's nominal voltage and its open-circuit voltage (OCV)?
o: Nominal is a label; OCV changes with SOC at rest
Nominal is measured under full load; OCV is fixed
They are always identical for LFP cells
OCV exists only for NMC chemistry
questions.why: Nominal voltage is a rounded reference (3.2 V for LFP). OCV is the rested terminal voltage and changes with SOC; the OCV-SOC curve is used in estimation. LFP's curve is very flat.

questions.q: Which ageing mechanism happens even while the battery sits idle?
o: Cycle ageing
Calendar ageing
Mechanical fatigue only
Deep discharge only
questions.why: Calendar ageing (for example SEI growth) continues over time and is accelerated by high temperature and high SOC, even without cycling.

questions.q: What describes thermal runaway?
o: Dendrites grow and stop once a short circuit forms
Self-heating feeds more heat release
Overcharge alone makes the cell voltage collapse
Electrolyte freezes and then cracks the cell case
questions.why: Thermal runaway is a positive feedback loop: heat triggers exothermic decomposition, releasing more heat. It can propagate from cell to cell.

questions.q: Lithium plating is most likely when…
o: Storing the pack at 50% SOC
Keeping all cells perfectly balanced
Discharging slowly at room temperature
Charging fast at low temperature
questions.why: At low temperature or high charge rate, lithium ions can't intercalate fast enough and deposit as metallic lithium on the anode, which loses capacity and can form dendrites.

questions.q: Why do operators often avoid holding a battery at 100% SOC for long periods?
o: It makes the pack heavier to lift
It lowers the open-circuit voltage
It switches off the BMS protection
High SOC speeds up calendar ageing
questions.why: High SOC means high anode/cathode stress, so parasitic reactions are faster. Many operators park at mid SOC when idle.

questions.q: What is the role of venting and gas detection in a container?
o: Lower the internal resistance of the cells
Balance the cell voltages inside each string
Cool the cells during ordinary charging and discharging
Detect off-gas early and keep it below explosive limits
questions.why: Early off-gas (hydrogen, CO, solvents) precedes thermal runaway. Detection and ventilation or explosion relief prevent a deflagration inside the enclosure.

questions.q: What is the main job of a power conversion system (PCS) in a BESS?
o: Stores firmware and event logs for the BMS
Removes heat from cells with liquid coolant
Monitors each cell voltage and temperature
Bidirectional DC/AC converter to the grid
questions.why: The PCS is a bidirectional inverter/rectifier: it charges the battery from AC and discharges DC into AC.

questions.q: In an IGBT inverter, what causes switching loss?
o: Gate drive current drawn from the auxiliary supply
Frequency of the voltage on the grid side
ESR losses in the DC bus capacitors alone
Voltage and current overlap during each transition
questions.why: During each transition the device carries current while blocking voltage, so energy is lost per switching event. Total switching loss grows with switching frequency.

questions.q: How does a grid-forming inverter differ from a grid-following one?
o: Following needs no DC source to deliver power
Forming sets voltage; following tracks the grid
Forming works only beside a diesel generator
Forming cannot supply any reactive power
questions.why: A grid-following inverter measures the grid angle with a PLL and injects current. A grid-forming inverter behaves like a voltage source, so it can support weak grids and island operation.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an LCL filter on an inverter output?
o: Attenuate switching harmonics before the grid
Measure the grid frequency for the phase-locked loop
Boost the DC bus voltage when SOC is low
Balance cell voltages within the string
questions.why: The inductor-capacitor-inductor network smooths the PWM waveform so current harmonics meet grid-code limits at lower size and cost than a single inductor.

questions.q: What is anti-islanding protection?
o: Keep cells from overheating in direct sun
Isolate one container from its neighbour in a fault
Detect grid loss and stop injecting power
Limit the charge rate as SOC nears full
questions.why: If the grid trips but a local source keeps energising the line, crews could be harmed. Inverters detect islanding and disconnect (unless designed for intentional islanding).

questions.q: Which three modes of heat transfer are there?
o: Conduction, convection and radiation
Compression, expansion and evaporation
Diffusion, filtration and sublimation
Induction, absorption and reflection
questions.why: Heat moves by conduction (through solids), convection (through moving fluid) and radiation (electromagnetic waves).

questions.q: A pump runs at half speed. By what factor does ideal power consumption change (affinity laws)?
questions.why: Flow scales with speed, head with speed squared and power with speed cubed: (1/2)³ = 1/8. That is why variable speed drives save so much energy.

questions.q: Why is a narrow cell temperature spread inside a pack desirable?
o: LFP cells work only at exactly 25 °C
Hotter cells age faster and imbalance spreads
It reduces the weight of the DC cabling
It removes the need for reactive power support
questions.why: Temperature spread causes different ageing rates and resistance between cells, so the weakest cell limits the string.

questions.q: Heat generated inside a cell during current flow is mainly…
o: Friction between the electrode layers during cycling
Chemical heat released by the electrolyte alone
Radiation from the container surface to the sky
Joule (I²R) heating plus reversible entropic heat
questions.why: Joule heating from internal resistance dominates, plus smaller reversible entropic heat. It scales with the square of current.

questions.q: What does thermal resistance (K/W) describe?
o: Electrical resistance of a cell at high temperature
Speed of coolant flow through a pipe
Temperature rise per watt along a heat path
Energy needed to warm one kilogram by one kelvin
questions.why: Thermal resistance is ΔT divided by heat flow, analogous to electrical resistance. Lower thermal resistance means heat moves more easily.

questions.q: What does thermal mass (heat capacity) do to a battery's temperature response?
o: Slows temperature change, buying time to react
Removes the need for any active cooling at all
Speeds up the response to load changes
Raises the terminal voltage of the cells under load
questions.why: A large thermal mass makes temperature rise more slowly for a given heat input, so short load spikes cause a small temperature change.

questions.q: Which four components make up a basic vapour-compression refrigeration cycle?
o: Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator
Pump, filter, radiator, accumulator, fan
Fan, heat sink, regulator, receiver, valve
Compressor, boiler, turbine, feed pump, fan
questions.why: The refrigerant is compressed, condensed (rejecting heat), expanded through a valve, and evaporated (absorbing heat) before returning to the compressor.

questions.q: In which component does the refrigerant absorb heat from the chilled-water loop?
o: Evaporator
Condenser
Compressor
Expansion valve
questions.why: Cold, low-pressure liquid refrigerant boils in the evaporator, taking heat from the water and cooling it.

questions.q: What does the compressor do to the refrigerant?
o: Raises pressure and temperature of the vapour
Turns vapour into liquid at constant pressure
Cools the vapour with outside air
Reduces the pressure of the liquid
questions.why: The compressor does work on the vapour, increasing pressure and temperature so it can reject heat to the ambient in the condenser.

questions.q: What happens in the condenser?
o: Liquid refrigerant boils and absorbs heat from water
Pressure drops across a metering valve, cooling it
Hot vapour rejects heat to air or water and condenses
Refrigerant gas is squeezed to a higher pressure
questions.why: The condenser rejects the heat absorbed in the evaporator plus compressor work into the ambient (air or cooling water) as vapour condenses to liquid.

questions.q: What does the expansion valve do, and which process does it represent on a pressure-enthalpy diagram?
o: Vapour is compressed at constant entropy
Heat is added at constant pressure
Heat is removed at constant temperature
Pressure drops at constant enthalpy
questions.why: Throttling reduces pressure with almost no heat exchange, so enthalpy is constant. Part of the liquid flashes to vapour and the mixture becomes cold.

questions.q: A chiller delivers 450 kW of cooling with a COP of 4.5. How much electrical power does it use?
o: 10 kW
45 kW
100 kW
questions.why: COP = cooling / electrical input, so input = 450 / 4.5 = 100 kW.

questions.q: Why does chiller COP usually fall when ambient temperature rises?
o: Higher condensing pressure raises compressor work
Hot refrigerant becomes less dense and lighter
The evaporator coil begins to freeze over
Circulation pumps start to run backwards
questions.why: Higher ambient raises condensing temperature and pressure. More compressor work per unit of cooling is needed, so COP drops.

questions.q: Why can raising the chilled-water supply setpoint (for example from 7 °C to 10 °C) improve efficiency?
o: The condenser is no longer needed
More refrigerant circulates through the cycle
Less lift, so less compressor work per kW
Ambient temperature drops by several degrees
questions.why: A warmer evaporating temperature narrows the gap between evaporator and condenser pressure. Less lift means less compressor work, at the cost of a smaller allowed temperature margin to the load.

questions.q: Why do variable-speed chillers often show their best efficiency at partial load?
o: Refrigerant flow stops completely during part load
Compressors spin faster to match the lower load
Heat exchangers are oversized for the duty
Lower load raises the pressure lift across the compressor
questions.why: At part load the heat exchangers are oversized for the duty, giving smaller temperature differences and lower lift. This is why IPLV or SEER, not full-load COP, describe real efficiency.

questions.q: What is superheat at the evaporator outlet?
o: Vapour temperature above saturation at that pressure
Temperature measured inside the condenser shell
Heat added to the vapour by the compressor motor
Liquid temperature below its saturation point
questions.why: Superheat ensures all liquid has evaporated so no liquid reaches the compressor. Too little risks liquid slugging, too much wastes evaporator area.

questions.q: What is subcooling at the condenser outlet?
o: Vapour heated above its saturation temperature
Liquid cooled below its saturation temperature
Compressor oil temperature margin
Cooling-tower water temperature drop
questions.why: Subcooling makes sure that only liquid reaches the expansion valve and increases cooling capacity per kg of refrigerant, avoiding flash gas before the valve.

questions.q: What is a cooling tower's approach temperature?
o: Leaving water temperature minus ambient wet-bulb
Condenser inlet temperature minus evaporator outlet
Entering water temperature minus leaving water
Ambient dry-bulb minus ambient wet-bulb temperature
questions.why: Approach is how closely the tower cools the water to the wet-bulb temperature, the theoretical limit. A small approach needs a larger tower.

questions.q: Why are water-cooled chillers often more efficient than air-cooled ones?
o: They consume less water than air-cooled units
Condensing happens against a lower, wet-bulb based temperature
They use a different refrigerant that needs no compressor
They run at a higher chilled-water temperature by design
questions.why: Wet-bulb temperature is lower than dry-bulb, so condensing pressure is lower and compressor work smaller, at the cost of water use and tower maintenance.

questions.q: What does a 'low delta-T syndrome' mean in a chilled-water loop?
o: The compressor motor overheats at low load
Evaporator water temperature falls below freezing
Return-supply difference below design, so flow rises
Loop pressure climbs above design limits at part load
questions.why: For the same heat load a smaller ΔT needs more flow. Pumps work harder and chillers can be loaded inefficiently.

questions.q: Water flows at 10 kg/s through a cooler and its temperature drops by 5 K (cp = 4.18 kJ/kg·K). How much heat is removed?
o: 42 kW
105 kW
209 kW
418 kW

questions.q: What is short cycling in a chiller?
o: Running the chiller only during the night
Operating while the ambient is very cold
A refrigeration cycle with fewer than four components
Frequent compressor starts and stops
questions.why: Short cycling arises when capacity exceeds the load or controls have a narrow deadband. Minimum run and off timers and staging logic prevent it.

questions.q: What is free cooling?
o: Cooling the loop with large blocks of stored ice
Cooling the loop with cold ambient air, no compressor
Adding extra compressors to share the cooling load
Running the chillers at night on cheaper power
questions.why: When ambient is cold enough, heat can be rejected directly via a dry cooler or economiser, so the compressor is off and cooling is nearly free.

questions.q: Why is glycol added to a coolant loop?
o: Raises heat capacity and lowers the viscosity
Makes the coolant electrically conductive for sensors
Removes the need for circulation pumps
Lowers freezing point but reduces heat capacity
questions.why: Glycol protects against freezing; the trade-off is a lower specific heat and higher viscosity, so more flow and pumping power are needed.

questions.q: Using a Carnot model, what is the maximum cooling COP for a cold side at 280 K and a hot side at 310 K?
questions.why: COP_Carnot = T_c / (T_h − T_c) = 280 / 30 ≈ 9.3. Real chillers reach a fraction of this.

questions.q: In a liquid-cooled BESS, why does thermal inertia of the coolant loop and cells matter for control?
o: Removes the need for temperature sensors
Pre-cool or delay chiller runtime within limits
Stops all heat generation inside the cells
Raises the chiller COP automatically at every load
questions.why: The thermal mass lets the chiller run when electricity is cheap or ambient is cool and coast during peaks, as long as cell temperature stays inside limits.

questions.q: In a chilled loop with fixed heat load, doubling the ΔT does what to the required flow?
o: Halves it
Doubles it
Leaves it unchanged
Quarters it
questions.why: Q = m·cp·ΔT: for fixed Q, flow is inversely proportional to ΔT. With pump power scaling roughly with flow cubed in variable-speed operation, savings can be large.

questions.q: What is compressor surge in a centrifugal chiller?
o: Rapid freezing of water in the evaporator
Flow reversal when lift exceeds capability
Refrigerant escaping past the shaft seal
A brief voltage spike on the motor supply
questions.why: At low load and high lift, the compressor can't sustain forward flow, causing violent pulsations that damage the machine. Hot-gas bypass and speed control avoid it.

questions.q: What does a refrigerant's GWP describe?
o: Gas weight carried per unit of pressure
Gauge working pressure of the whole system
Gravimetric water content measured in the oil
Warming effect compared with CO₂ if released
questions.why: GWP compares the warming impact of a refrigerant leak with the same mass of CO₂ over a set horizon. Regulations are phasing down high-GWP refrigerants.

questions.q: What is Coulomb counting?
o: Measuring insulation resistance to earth
Measuring cell temperature with a surface probe
Integrating current over time to track SOC
Counting the full charge cycles used per year
questions.why: SOC(t) = SOC(0) + (1/Q)∫I dt. It is simple but drifts because of sensor offset, so it needs periodic correction.

questions.q: Why is an extended Kalman filter often used for SOC estimation?
o: Replaces the pack with one fixed resistor
Makes the current sensor completely unnecessary
Controls the cell temperature directly via the chiller
Fuses current integration with a voltage model
questions.why: The EKF predicts SOC from current and corrects it with the terminal voltage through a nonlinear battery model, balancing drift against noise.

questions.q: In a PID controller, what is integral windup?
o: Integral term keeps growing at actuator limits
Proportional gain is set far too low for the plant
Setpoint oscillates around its target value
Derivative term amplifies measurement noise
questions.why: When output is limited (for example max power) the integral keeps accumulating error. After the limit clears, the large stored value causes overshoot. Anti-windup clamps or back-calculates it.

questions.q: What does a droop control characteristic do for frequency support?
o: Power changes in proportion to frequency deviation
Voltage doubles whenever frequency rises
Power stays fixed whatever the frequency does
The converter trips at any frequency deviation
questions.why: Droop (for example 5%) maps frequency error to power change, so many units share the response automatically without communication.

questions.q: What does a battery equivalent-circuit (Thévenin) model include?
o: One lone capacitor connected in series with a load
Heat transfer equations for each cell in the pack
A single fixed voltage source and nothing else
OCV source, series resistance, RC pairs
questions.why: An OCV source with series resistance and one or more RC branches reproduces voltage relaxation after load changes, and is the basis of many SOC and SOH estimators.

questions.q: What does grid frequency drifting below 50 Hz (or 60 Hz) tell you?
o: Demand exceeds generation
Generation exceeds demand
Voltage is too high
A transformer has failed
questions.why: Frequency falls when consumption is higher than generation as rotating machines slow down. Reserves and batteries inject power to restore balance.

questions.q: What is system inertia and why does it matter more with more renewables?
o: Resistance of the long transmission cables
Stored rotating energy that slows frequency swings
Delay between market bids and physical delivery
Total weight of the installed battery containers
questions.why: Synchronous machines provide kinetic energy that resists frequency changes. Inverter-based resources provide none unless they emulate it, so the same imbalance moves frequency faster.

questions.q: Which organisation is usually responsible for operating the high-voltage transmission grid?
o: The transmission system operator (TSO)
The electricity retailer
The distribution system operator (DSO)
The power exchange operator
questions.why: TSOs run the high-voltage network and balance the system. DSOs run lower-voltage local networks.

questions.q: What is black start capability?
o: Ride through a complete loss of auxiliary lighting
Limit the fault current seen on a feeder
Restart with no grid supply and energise the network
Keep running at zero load without tripping
questions.why: Black start units can start from standstill using their own storage or generator and help rebuild the grid after a blackout. Grid-forming batteries can provide this.

questions.q: What is a ramp rate limit?
o: Maximum allowed change in power, e.g. MW per minute
Maximum current rating of a power cable in amps
Minimum market price allowed per MWh sold
Battery depth-of-discharge limit per cycle
questions.why: Ramp limits stop sudden output changes that would stress the grid. Batteries can ramp very fast, so limits are usually set by the grid code or contract.

questions.q: What is the day-ahead market?
o: A fixed-price contract signed years ahead
Auction on the previous day setting price and volume per period
Continuous trading seconds before delivery on a live book
A market that trades natural gas only
questions.why: Participants submit bids and offers. The exchange clears the market once, and gives each period (hour or 15 minutes) a price for the next day.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the intraday market?
o: Trade capacity commitments for the coming year
Settle imbalances after the delivery period ends
Adjust positions near delivery as forecasts change
Set the electricity price for the following year
questions.why: Intraday trading is continuous or in auctions after day-ahead, letting participants correct for forecast errors, outages and new information.

questions.q: What is energy arbitrage for a battery?
o: Reduce demand charges behind the customer meter
Charge when prices are low, discharge when high
Sell frequency reserves to the transmission operator
Offer black start capability to the grid
questions.why: The profit is the price spread between discharge and charge periods, less efficiency losses and degradation cost.

questions.q: A battery buys at €40/MWh and sells at €110/MWh with 85% round-trip efficiency. What is the profit per MWh sold?
questions.why: To sell 1 MWh you must buy 1/0.85 = 1.176 MWh, costing about €47. Profit = 110 − 47 ≈ €63 per MWh sold, before degradation and fees.

questions.q: Why must the price spread exceed more than just the round-trip loss for arbitrage to pay?
o: Spreads are always zero in practice anyway
Degradation and fees add cost on every cycle
Batteries cannot charge during the night hours
Regulators fix all of the wholesale prices
questions.why: Each cycle consumes cell life and incurs fees and auxiliary energy. The spread must cover energy losses plus these marginal costs for the cycle to add value.

questions.q: What is FCR (frequency containment reserve)?
o: A financial hedge contract on power prices
Capacity payment for building new power plants
Fast automatic response to frequency deviations
Slow manual reserve called by telephone
questions.why: FCR responds within seconds proportionally to frequency deviation. Batteries are well suited because they respond almost instantly.

questions.q: How does aFRR differ from FCR?
o: Responds faster than FCR, within under a second
A paper contract with no physical delivery
Is traded only in the day-ahead auction each day
Follows a TSO setpoint to restore frequency
questions.why: FCR is local proportional response; aFRR is activated centrally via control signal over some minutes to bring frequency back to nominal and release FCR.

questions.q: What characterises mFRR (manual frequency restoration reserve)?
o: Called by the TSO over minutes for lasting imbalances
Continuous trading for the next delivery hour
Sub-second automatic response to frequency
Automatic droop response within seconds
questions.why: mFRR bids are activated by TSO instruction (minutes), relieving aFRR when imbalances persist.

questions.q: In ancillary markets paid for capacity availability, what must the operator do?
o: Keep headroom and SOC within bounds to deliver
Avoid ever being activated by the TSO operator
Keep the battery at 100% SOC at all times
Disconnect from the grid right after bidding
questions.why: Capacity payments are for being able to deliver. The operator must manage SOC so both up and down response remain possible during the product window.

questions.q: What is revenue stacking?
o: Buying more batteries to raise the MW rating
Selling only into one single market all year
Earning from several services by splitting time
Counting the same revenue twice in two markets
questions.why: A battery can do arbitrage in some hours and reserves in others, but the same MW cannot be sold to two markets at the same time.

questions.q: Why can wholesale prices go negative?
o: Batteries are discharging into the grid
Exchange rates move sharply overnight
Inflexible output exceeds demand
Regulators subsidise consumers directly
questions.why: When must-run or subsidised output exceeds demand, sellers pay to offload. A battery earns by charging at negative prices.

questions.q: In a marginal-pricing (merit order) market, what sets the clearing price?
o: The cheapest offer in the stack
The offer of the last unit needed
The average of all accepted bids
The highest bid from any single buyer
questions.why: Offers are ranked by price. Supply is accepted until demand is met, and the marginal accepted offer sets the uniform price for all accepted bids.

questions.q: What is the 'duck curve'?
o: A chart of battery capacity ageing over time
Net load dips at midday, then ramps steeply
A plant maintenance schedule through the year
A histogram of grid frequency values
questions.why: High solar output pushes net demand down at midday. Evening ramps are steep as solar fades, creating price spreads that batteries exploit.

questions.q: What happens to arbitrage spreads as more batteries enter the same market?
o: They invert, so batteries stop trading in that market
They stay flat, since storage hardly moves clearing prices
They widen as storage makes peak prices spike
They compress as charging lifts and discharging lowers prices
questions.why: Charging lifts off-peak prices and discharging lowers peak prices. Revenue per MW falls as the market saturates.

questions.q: How does battery duration affect arbitrage revenue per MWh?
o: Revenue is fixed per MW installed
Longer duration earns proportionally more
Short durations capture the best spreads
Duration has no effect on revenue
questions.why: The first hour of discharge captures the best prices. Additional hours earn progressively smaller spreads.

questions.q: Why is a perfect-foresight backtest an upper bound on arbitrage revenue?
o: Live dispatch assumes zero conversion losses
Live dispatch uses forecasts that contain errors
Live dispatch ignores the price signal entirely
Live dispatch uses far more full cycles per day
questions.why: Perfect foresight knows all prices ahead of time. Real dispatch uses forecasts, so realised revenue is lower. The ratio is a measure of how good the forecasts are.

questions.q: What is peak shaving behind the meter?
o: Charge the battery during the grid's peak hours
Offer black start capability to the grid operator
Sell stored energy on the wholesale market
Cut the highest peaks to lower demand charges
questions.why: Many tariffs bill on the highest kW demand in a period. Discharging during the peak lowers that billed value.

questions.q: What is a tolling agreement for a battery?
o: An annual charge levied for the grid connection
A reserve product paying for availability, not energy
Owner dispatches freely and keeps all revenue
Offtaker dispatches for a fixed fee; owner avoids price risk
questions.why: The offtaker takes market risk and pays a fixed capacity-like fee. The owner keeps operational risk (availability, degradation).

questions.q: How do nodal (locational marginal) prices differ from zonal prices?
o: Zonal prices are set separately per household
They are identical everywhere on the grid at all times
Nodal prices differ by location when lines congest
Nodal prices ignore losses on the network entirely
questions.why: In nodal markets each bus has its own price, reflecting congestion and losses. Zonal markets use one price per large zone and handle congestion separately.

questions.q: What does a capacity market pay for?
o: Fuel purchases made by power plants
Frequency measurements sent to the TSO
Energy delivered in each individual hour
Being available during system stress
questions.why: A capacity market pays a fixed amount for committed availability so enough resource exists at peak, independent of how much energy is sold.

questions.q: What is an imbalance settlement?
o: A fee charged for access to the transmission grid
An auction for reserve capacity a day ahead
A tax on profits earned from trading energy
Paying or receiving a price for deviating from schedule
questions.why: Parties are responsible for their schedule. Deviations are settled at the imbalance price, which can be punitive in the direction that hurts the system.

questions.q: What is the difference between MW and MWh in a battery contract?
o: MW is power capacity; MWh is stored energy
MW measures voltage and MWh measures current
They are two names for one and the same unit
MW is energy while MWh is power capacity
questions.why: Power (MW) limits how fast you can charge or discharge; energy (MWh) is how much you can store. Duration = MWh / MW.

questions.q: In a Modbus system, which device initiates requests?
o: The slave (server)
The master (client)
The broker that routes the messages
The sensor that publishes the value
questions.why: Modbus is request-response: the master polls and the slave replies. Modern terminology is client and server.

questions.q: How should a telemetry gap shorter than a minute be treated when computing energy?
o: Treat the gap as zero power for that period
Double the next measured value to compensate
Delete the whole day from the dataset
Hold or interpolate, and flag it as imputed
questions.why: Short gaps are usually bridged by hold or interpolation while keeping a data-quality flag, so downstream calculations know it was not measured.

questions.q: What is the role of a battery management system (BMS)?
o: Trade energy on the electricity market
Convert DC to AC for the grid connection
Monitor cells and protect them within limits
Cool the container using the chiller plant
questions.why: The BMS measures voltages and temperatures, estimates SOC and SOH, balances cells and opens contactors when limits are breached.

questions.q: What is the difference between an EMS and a BMS?
o: The EMS protects the cells; the BMS dispatches the whole site
The EMS dispatches the whole site; the BMS protects the cells
They are two names for the same controller
The EMS measures cell voltages; the BMS submits market bids
questions.why: The BMS acts at cell and rack level for safety. The EMS decides what the whole plant should do (power setpoints, schedules, market signals) within BMS limits.

questions.q: Why does timestamp quality matter in telemetry?
o: Timestamps reduce the storage space needed
Timestamps change the measured voltage values
The timestamp sets the market price directly
Clock errors break joins and event ordering
questions.why: Derivatives, energy integration and cause-effect ordering across devices rely on consistent time. Use UTC, synced clocks and track source vs ingestion time.

questions.q: A test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity, and the disease prevalence is 1%. Given a positive result, roughly what is the probability of disease?
questions.why: Per 10,000 people: 100 sick (99 test positive), 9,900 healthy (99 false positives). P = 99 / 198 = 50%. Base rates dominate (Bayes' rule).

questions.q: The standard deviation is…
o: The mean absolute error
The variance squared
Half of the range of the data
Square root of the variance
questions.why: SD = √Var, and it has the same units as the data, unlike variance.

questions.q: Two variables have zero covariance. Which statement is correct?
o: A linear function of each other
Independent
Perfectly correlated
Dependent, just not linearly
questions.why: Zero covariance only rules out linear association. Y = X² with symmetric X has zero covariance with X but is fully dependent on it.

questions.q: What does the central limit theorem say, loosely?
o: The variance of any dataset equals one
Means of many samples become roughly normal
Any single sample is normally distributed
Medians always converge towards the sample mean
questions.why: For i.i.d. data with finite variance the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as n grows, which justifies many confidence intervals.

questions.q: What does a 95% confidence interval mean?
o: 95% of all the data lies inside the interval
About 95% of such intervals contain the true value
A 95% chance that this sample mean is exact
The true value moves around inside the interval
questions.why: Confidence refers to the long-run coverage of the method, not to the probability that this particular interval contains the parameter (that is a Bayesian credible interval).

questions.q: What does a p-value of 0.03 mean?
o: The effect is 97% likely to be real and large
Such extreme data occurs ~3% of the time under the null
The null hypothesis has a 3% chance of being true
The test has 3% statistical power to detect it
questions.why: A p-value is P(data at least this extreme | null). It is not the probability that the null is true.

questions.q: Which describes a Gaussian process?
o: Ensemble of decision trees voting on labels
Fixed-degree polynomial fitted by least squares
Clustering method based on density peaks
Prior over functions set by a mean and a kernel
questions.why: A GP places a prior over functions with covariance given by a kernel; the posterior gives predictions with uncertainty.

questions.q: When is the median a better summary than the mean?
o: Skewed data or outliers
Perfectly symmetric data
Data with zero variance
Categorical labels
questions.why: The median is robust to extreme values, while the mean is pulled by them. Income and latency are typical examples.

questions.q: What does it mean for a time series to be (weakly) stationary?
o: Constant mean and variance, lag-based autocovariance
Constant value at every time step, no variation
Values that increase steadily with a fixed slope
Values that contain no missing points or noise
questions.why: Weak stationarity needs time-invariant mean and variance, and autocovariance that depends only on the lag. Trend or seasonality breaks it.

questions.q: In a Kalman filter, what happens if you increase the process noise covariance Q?
o: It stops updating the state estimate altogether
It trusts new measurements more and reacts faster
It trusts the model more and smooths harder
It ignores every new measurement it receives
questions.why: A larger Q means the model is less certain, so the Kalman gain rises and the estimate follows measurements more closely, with more noise.

questions.q: What does differencing a time series usually remove?
o: Seasonality at every possible period
Trend (non-stationarity in the mean)
All random noise in the series
Outliers only
questions.why: Taking x_t − x_{t−1} removes a linear trend and often produces a stationary series. Seasonal differencing uses the seasonal lag.

questions.q: What does a slowly decaying autocorrelation function suggest?
o: Pure white noise with no structure at all
Absence of any outliers in the series
A series with no memory of its past values
Non-stationarity or a strong trend
questions.why: White noise has near-zero autocorrelation at all non-zero lags. Slow decay is typical for trending (unit-root) series.

questions.q: What is a Markov chain?
o: The sequence is fully deterministic given a seed
Steps are independent of each other like coin flips
The process remembers its entire history
Next state depends only on the current state
questions.why: The Markov property says the future is independent of the past given the present, which makes models tractable.

questions.q: How is a random walk different from white noise?
o: Variance grows with time as noise accumulates
White noise has a built-in upward trend
A random walk has constant zero variance over time
They are the same process described differently
questions.why: A random walk is the sum of white-noise steps and is non-stationary. White noise is a sequence of uncorrelated shocks with constant variance.

questions.q: Why can shuffled k-fold cross-validation mislead on time series?
o: Folds become too small to compute any metric
It requires labels that are not yet known
Future information leaks into training
The scores are unbiased but very noisy
questions.why: Neighbouring points are correlated, so random folds train on the future. Use forward-chaining (rolling origin) splits instead.

questions.q: What is the main effect of L1 regularization?
o: Removes outliers from the training data
Makes the input features orthogonal
Doubles the learning rate during training
Shrinks some weights exactly to zero
questions.why: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero, so many coefficients become exactly zero. L2 shrinks smoothly without producing zeros.

questions.q: Training error is very low and validation error is high. What does this indicate?
o: Underfitting: make the model simpler
Overfitting: add data or regularise
Label noise in every single case
A learning rate that is too low
questions.why: A large train-validation gap means high variance (overfitting). Remedies include more data, regularization, early stopping or a simpler model.

questions.q: Why is the precision-recall curve often more informative than ROC on imbalanced data?
o: Many negatives dilute ROC's false-positive rate
PR curves are cheaper to compute on large sets
ROC cannot be computed on imbalanced data
PR curves ignore the positive class altogether
questions.why: With many negatives, even a tiny false-positive rate can mean many false alarms relative to true positives. Precision exposes that.

questions.q: What principle does empirical risk minimisation describe?
o: Minimise average training loss as a proxy for expected loss
Minimise the number of parameters in the model
Maximise the margin between classes on training data
Minimise the loss on the test set directly
questions.why: ERM picks the model with the lowest average training loss, hoping it generalises. Regularisation controls the gap.

questions.q: What is the bias-variance trade-off?
o: Variance only exists for linear models
Bias and variance are one single quantity
Simple models have high bias, flexible ones high variance
More data always raises the variance of a model
questions.why: Error splits into bias (systematic miss), variance (sensitivity to the sample) and noise. Model complexity trades one for the other.

questions.q: What is data leakage?
o: Classes are heavily imbalanced between train and test
Information not available at prediction time sneaks into the features
Missing values appear in the training data
The model memorises the data because it has too many parameters
questions.why: Examples are using future values, target-derived features, or fitting preprocessing on all data. Leakage inflates validation scores and fails in production.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a held-out test set?
o: Unbiased estimate on unseen data
Removing outliers from the training data
Tuning the hyperparameters of the model
Increasing the size of the training set
questions.why: The test set must stay untouched until the end. If you tune on it, the estimate becomes optimistic.

questions.q: In fraud detection, missing a fraud is far worse than a false alarm. Which metric should you emphasise?
o: Accuracy
Recall
Specificity
R²
questions.why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) measures how many true cases are caught, so it should be prioritised, usually while watching precision.

questions.q: How do random forests and gradient boosting differ in combining trees?
o: Forests add trees to fix errors; boosting averages independent trees
Forests average independent trees; boosting adds trees to fix errors
Forests grow one tree; boosting grows a hundred
Both average independent trees but boosting uses deeper ones
questions.why: Random forests reduce variance by averaging decorrelated deep trees. Boosting reduces bias by fitting each shallow tree to previous errors.

questions.q: What does backpropagation compute?
o: Gradients of the loss via the chain rule
The optimal weights in closed form directly
A random initialisation of the weights
The best learning rate for each separate layer
questions.why: Backprop efficiently applies the chain rule to give gradients, which an optimizer such as SGD uses to update weights.

questions.q: What does logistic regression output?
o: The depth of a decision tree
A cluster label for each row
A probability between 0 and 1
An unbounded real number only
questions.why: A linear score is passed through the sigmoid to produce a probability, trained by minimising log loss.

questions.q: Why does a deep decision tree tend to overfit?
o: It makes almost no splits at all in practice
It cannot accept numeric inputs without scaling
It has too few leaves to fit the training data
It memorises noise with very specific rules
questions.why: Unbounded depth lets the tree memorise samples. Pruning, depth limits or ensembles reduce variance.

questions.q: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
o: Gradients shrink through layers so early ones barely learn
The loss reaches exactly zero and training halts
Gradients grow through layers and weights blow up
Training data runs out before the loss converges
questions.why: Repeated multiplication by small derivatives (sigmoid/tanh) makes gradients tiny. ReLU, residual connections and normalisation mitigate it.

questions.q: What does the learning rate control in gradient descent?
o: Choice of the loss function used in training
Mini-batch size used for each update step
Step size along the negative gradient
Number of layers in the network architecture
questions.why: Too small is slow, too large overshoots or diverges. Schedules and adaptive optimizers adjust it.

questions.q: What does PCA find?
o: Orthogonal directions of maximum variance
The best classifier for labelled training data
Nonlinear manifolds embedded in the data
Clusters of similar points in feature space
questions.why: PCA finds orthogonal directions (principal components) ordered by explained variance, the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

questions.q: What does k-means do?
o: Detects outliers in the data and nothing else
Predicts a continuous target value from features
Assigns points to k clusters by distance to centres
Finds the largest eigenvector of the data
questions.why: It alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids. It assumes roughly spherical clusters and needs k.

questions.q: How does Isolation Forest flag anomalies?
o: It fits a single normal distribution to the data
Anomalies are isolated in fewer random splits
It measures local density in every grid cell
It removes the biggest cluster first, then repeats
questions.why: Random trees split features randomly. Rare, different points are separated quickly, giving short average path lengths and high anomaly scores.

questions.q: Why might a z-score threshold fail for anomaly detection on telemetry?
o: Telemetry is always perfectly Gaussian
Drift, seasonality and heavy tails break the assumption
Z-scores cannot be computed on sensor data
Z-scores need labelled anomalies to work
questions.why: Drifting baselines and daily cycles make a global mean and SD misleading. Use rolling or condition-aware baselines and robust statistics.

questions.q: Which property makes a convex problem attractive?
o: Any local minimum is a global minimum
It requires all variables to be integers
It cannot have any constraints at all
It always has a purely linear objective
questions.why: For a convex objective on a convex set, local optimum equals global optimum, so gradient-based methods are reliable.

questions.q: Deciding which chillers to switch on or off each hour, plus their loads, is best modelled as…
o: linear regression
a mixed-integer linear program
principal component analysis
gradient descent on a neural net
questions.why: On/off decisions are binary variables, loads are continuous, constraints are linear: a MILP.

questions.q: What does model predictive control (MPC) do at each step?
o: Solve over a horizon, apply the first move, then re-solve
Estimate the state and leave control to the operator
Train a neural network on live data each step
Apply a fixed PID law tuned once at commissioning
questions.why: MPC solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem using a model and forecasts, applies the first action, then re-solves with new measurements (receding horizon).

questions.q: What defines a linear program (LP)?
o: Linear objective and constraints, continuous variables
A problem solved only by gradient descent methods
Any problem that contains integer variables
A problem with a quadratic objective
questions.why: LPs are convex and solved reliably at large scale by simplex or interior-point methods. Battery dispatch with constant efficiency is a classic LP.

questions.q: What is the shadow price (dual value) of a constraint?
o: The slope of the loss curve at the optimum
Objective change per unit relaxation of the constraint
A penalty applied when constraints are infeasible
The running cost of the solver per iteration
questions.why: It tells you what an extra unit of the limited resource would be worth, for example the value of one more MWh of battery capacity.

questions.q: What typically happens if the gradient descent learning rate is too large?
o: The solution is guaranteed global
The loss function becomes convex
Convergence to the optimum is guaranteed
The iterates oscillate or diverge
questions.why: Steps overshoot the minimum. For a quadratic, step sizes above 2/L (L is curvature) diverge.

questions.q: How does the simplex method differ from an interior-point method?
o: Simplex walks vertices; interior point crosses the interior
Simplex handles only nonlinear problems
Interior point works only on integer variables
They are the same algorithm by another name
questions.why: Both solve LPs. Simplex is often fast in practice; interior-point has polynomial guarantees and scales well on large sparse problems.

questions.q: What can you do about local minima in a non-convex problem?
o: Remove the objective function and re-run
Several starting points or global methods
Nothing can be done about them
Raise the learning rate toward infinity
questions.why: Multi-start, simulated annealing, basin hopping or relaxations improve the odds, but give no guarantee of global optimality.

questions.q: What does weak duality state?
o: Dual feasible values bound the primal optimum
Only integer problems have duals at all
The dual is always larger than the primal
Primal and dual problems are unrelated
questions.why: For a minimisation problem, the dual objective is a lower bound on the primal optimum. The gap is zero (strong duality) for convex problems under mild conditions.

questions.q: What do the KKT conditions provide for a convex problem?
o: A heuristic for choosing starting points
A guarantee that all variables are integers
A bound on the largest usable learning rate
Necessary and sufficient optimality conditions (convex)
questions.why: Stationarity, primal and dual feasibility and complementary slackness together characterise the optimum for convex problems.

questions.q: What is an LP relaxation of a MILP used for?
o: A bound that branch and bound builds on
The exact integer optimum every time
A version with all constraints removed
An exact solver for non-convex problems
questions.why: Dropping integrality yields an LP whose optimum bounds the MILP. Branch and bound splits on fractional variables and prunes with those bounds.

questions.q: What is a quadratic program (QP)?
o: Any integer program
Quadratic objective with linear constraints
A gradient-free search method
Linear objective with quadratic constraints only
questions.why: QPs appear in portfolio problems, regularised regression and MPC with quadratic tracking cost. They are convex if the quadratic form is positive semidefinite.

questions.q: In two-stage stochastic programming, what is decided in the first stage?
o: Only the random seed of the solver
The probabilities of the scenarios
Decisions made before uncertainty is revealed
Decisions made after all uncertainty is known
questions.why: First-stage decisions (for example day-ahead bids) must be made before prices or demand are known. Second-stage recourse actions adapt to each scenario.

questions.q: What does robust optimisation optimise?
o: The median scenario in the uncertainty set
The expected value over all the scenarios
The best case outcome across scenarios
Worst case over an uncertainty set
questions.why: It guarantees feasibility and a bound on cost for every realisation in the uncertainty set, at the price of conservatism.

questions.q: What does dynamic programming exploit?
o: Convexity of the objective function only
Optimal substructure of the problem
The simplex method on the problem
Random sampling of the possible states
questions.why: Bellman's principle: the remaining decisions must be optimal from any state. Battery scheduling over an SOC grid is a typical DP.

questions.q: How does Newton's method differ from gradient descent?
o: It is cheaper per step because it never inverts anything
It needs no derivatives, just function evaluations
It uses only the sign of the gradient and takes fixed steps
It uses curvature (the Hessian) and converges fast near the optimum
questions.why: Newton scales steps by the inverse Hessian, which converges very fast near the solution but is costlier per step.

questions.q: What is a risk of a very large big-M constant in a MILP?
o: A weak relaxation and numerical trouble
Integrality of the variables is dropped silently
Constraints are silently removed from the model
The model automatically becomes convex
questions.why: Large M makes the relaxation loose, so branch-and-bound explores many nodes, and numerical errors can allow small violations. Use the tightest valid M.

questions.q: In a battery dispatch LP, why might the optimiser charge and discharge at the same time?
o: It lowers the terminal cell voltage
With negative prices, wasting energy can pay
Batteries physically cannot do it at all
It is always optimal to do so regardless of price
questions.why: When extra energy has a negative price, simultaneous charge and discharge wastes energy through losses and 'earns' the negative price. A binary or a penalty prevents this.

questions.q: Which problem class is generally NP-hard?
o: Mixed-integer programming
Linear programming
Least squares
Convex quadratic programming
questions.why: General MILP is NP-hard. LP and convex QP can be solved in polynomial time.

questions.q: When would you use a genetic algorithm?
o: A proof of global optimality is required
The problem is a large convex linear program
The problem has no decision variables to tune
Gradients unavailable and a rugged landscape
questions.why: Metaheuristics work on black-box or discrete problems but offer no optimality guarantee and need many evaluations.

questions.q: What is a Pareto front?
o: The single cheapest feasible solution
Solutions where improving one objective hurts another
The set of points that violate constraints
A plot of solver convergence per iteration
questions.why: In multi-objective problems, Pareto-optimal solutions are non-dominated. The trade-off, such as cost versus degradation, is chosen from the front.

questions.q: What is Bayesian optimisation best suited for?
o: Sorting very large arrays as fast as possible
Very large linear programs with many constraints
Convex problems with known, cheap gradients
Expensive black-box functions, few evaluations
questions.why: A surrogate model (often a GP) guides where to evaluate next, balancing exploration and exploitation. Common for hyperparameter tuning.

questions.q: What does a soft constraint do in an optimisation?
o: Allows violation at a penalty cost
Removes the variable from the model
Forces exact satisfaction of the limit
Makes the problem integer
questions.why: Penalty terms keep the problem feasible when hard limits conflict. The weights decide the trade-off.

questions.q: What is a confounder?
o: Is a duplicated row somewhere in the data
Is a random error term in the regression
Affects both treatment and outcome
Is the outcome variable itself being studied
questions.why: A confounder creates a spurious association between treatment and outcome unless controlled for, or unless randomisation breaks the link.

questions.q: Why does randomisation support causal conclusions in an A/B test?
o: It balances confounders between the groups
It guarantees statistical significance
It removes all of the noise from the outcome
It increases the total sample size available
questions.why: Random assignment makes treatment independent of other factors, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.

questions.q: What is statistical power?
o: Chance that the observed effect is due to noise
Chance of rejecting the null when it is true
Chance of detecting a real effect of a given size
The p-value threshold chosen before the test
questions.why: Power = 1 − β. Low power means real effects are often missed. It rises with sample size, effect size and lower noise.

questions.q: What problem arises from checking an A/B test repeatedly and stopping once p < 0.05?
o: Higher statistical power
Lower variance
A smaller sample size
Inflated false positives
questions.why: Repeated peeking is multiple testing. Use fixed horizons or sequential methods with adjusted thresholds.

questions.q: What is the leakage mistake when fitting a scaler?
o: Using standard scaling at all on features
Fitting it on all data before the split
Scaling the target variable as well
Using min-max scaling instead of z-scores
questions.why: Fit preprocessing on training data only and apply to validation/test; otherwise test statistics leak into training.

questions.q: Why do we seed random number generators in experiments?
o: To prevent overfitting of the final model
To make the results look better in reports
To make runs reproducible
To speed up the training of the model
questions.why: A fixed seed makes stochastic steps (splits, initialisation) repeatable so differences between runs can be attributed to your changes.

questions.q: How can lag features help for energy time series?
o: They give the model recent values as inputs
They remove seasonality from the target
They sort rows by time so that folds are fair
They add noise that regularises the model
questions.why: Lagged values, rolling means and calendar features supply the temporal context a tabular model lacks. Make sure lags are available at prediction time.

questions.q: What is a sensible way to treat missing sensor values?
o: Fill all gaps with zero so the series stays continuous
Drop every row that has any missing value
Find out why values are missing, then impute or flag them
Ignore them since models handle gaps by themselves
questions.why: Missingness can carry information (sensor offline). Use hold, interpolation or model-based imputation and add a missing indicator when appropriate.

questions.q: Which signal detects that live inputs no longer resemble training data?
o: A rising training loss during retraining runs
Drift metrics such as PSI or a KS test on features
Utilisation of the GPUs that serve the model
The count of commits to the model repository
questions.why: Drift monitoring compares live feature distributions against a reference, warning before performance metrics (which need labels) are available.

questions.q: What does epistemic uncertainty represent?
o: Label noise in the training set only
Irreducible noise that is inherent in the data
Rounding error in the floating-point arithmetic
Uncertainty from limited data, reducible with more
questions.why: Epistemic uncertainty concerns the model; aleatoric is inherent randomness. GPs and ensembles express epistemic uncertainty.

questions.q: What is a model registry for?
o: Version models with metadata so deployments are traceable
Schedule retraining jobs at fixed times
Store raw sensor data for later feature engineering
Run SQL queries against training tables
questions.why: A registry tracks versions, metrics, lineage and stage (staging, production) so you can roll back and audit.

questions.q: What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?
o: Data drift shifts the inputs; concept drift shifts input-to-output behaviour
Data drift is random noise; concept drift is a bug in the code
Data drift shifts the labels; concept drift shifts only the features
Data drift appears after retraining; concept drift appears before it
questions.why: With concept drift the same inputs now map to different outputs, for example degradation changes a battery's behaviour, so retraining is needed even if inputs look similar.

questions.q: What is a sensible way to deploy a new model safely?
o: Shadow or canary it against the current model
Deploy only on Friday afternoons when traffic is low
Skip testing and deploy everywhere at once
Replace the old model immediately in all regions
questions.why: Shadow mode runs the new model silently; canary exposes a small slice of traffic. Compare metrics before full rollout, and keep rollback ready.

questions.q: What is a risk of using an LLM to answer questions about internal documents without retrieval?
o: It will answer far too quickly for users to read
It will refuse to answer every question asked
It may invent plausible but wrong content
It will leak GPU memory contents to other users
questions.why: Without grounding, the model may invent facts. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies sources and allows citation and checks.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this function?
o: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
questions.why: A set lookup and insert are O(1) on average, so one pass over n items is O(n). With a list, the check would be O(n) and the total O(n²).

O(n³)
questions.why: The inner loop runs n−i times, so the total is n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2, which is O(n²).

o: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)
questions.why: `x in ys` on a list scans up to n elements for each of n items, so O(n²). Making ys a set gives O(n).

questions.q: What is the complexity of this loop?
o: O(n)
O(log n)
O(√n)
O(n log n)
questions.why: The value is halved every iteration, so it runs log₂ n times.

questions.q: What is the complexity of the following, with sizes n and m?
questions.code:
def g(a, b):
    for x in a:       # n items
        print(x)
    for y in b:       # m items
        print(y)
o: O(n·m)
O(n + m)
O(max(n, m)²)
O(log(n + m))
questions.why: The loops are sequential, not nested, so costs add: O(n + m).

questions.q: Appending to a Python list is described as amortized O(1). What does that mean?
o: It is constant only for lists under 1,000 items
Every single append takes exactly constant time
Each individual append takes O(log n) time
Rare resizes cost more; the average stays constant
questions.why: Resizing copies the array occasionally, but capacity grows geometrically, so the total cost over n appends is O(n).

questions.q: What is the complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n items?
o: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.why: Each step halves the search interval, so about log₂ n comparisons are needed.

questions.q: What is the complexity of this function?
o: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)
questions.why: Each call spawns two calls with n−1, so the call tree doubles in depth n: O(2ⁿ). Memoisation would make it O(n).

questions.q: Which data structure gives average O(1) lookup by key?
o: Binary heap (priority queue)
Linked list of nodes
Sorted list of keys
Hash table (dict)
questions.why: A hash table computes the slot from the key. Sorted lists need O(log n), linked lists O(n).

questions.q: What is the complexity of sorting n items with a comparison sort in general?
o: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²) at best
O(log n)
questions.why: Comparison sorts have an O(n log n) lower bound. Python's Timsort achieves it in the worst case.

questions.q: When is a heap a good choice?
o: Checking whether a value is present quickly
Repeatedly getting the smallest or largest item
Looking up arbitrary keys in constant time
Keeping elements in their insertion order
questions.why: A binary heap gives O(log n) push/pop and O(1) peek of the minimum, ideal for priority queues and top-k.

def add(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return bag

print(add(1))
print(add(2))
o: [1] then [1]
[1] then [2]
It raises an error
questions.why: The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared across calls. Use None as the default and create the list inside.

questions.q: Which is true about dictionary ordering in Python 3.7+?
o: Order is random each run
Insertion order is preserved
Keys are always sorted
Order depends on the hash only
questions.why: Since Python 3.7 insertion order is part of the language guarantee.

questions.q: Which method is called first when an instance is created?
o: __init__
__new__
__call__
__del__
questions.why: `__new__` allocates and returns the instance, then `__init__` initialises it. Overriding `__new__` is needed for singletons or immutable subclasses.

questions.q: Why catch a specific exception instead of a bare `except:`?
o: It suppresses every traceback automatically
A bare except hides bugs and catches Ctrl-C
Specific handlers execute noticeably faster
Python's grammar rejects a bare except
questions.why: A bare except catches BaseException subclasses too, such as Ctrl-C and SystemExit. Catch the narrowest exception you can actually handle.

questions.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
o: Tuples can be resized in place when needed
Lists cannot hold items of mixed types
Tuples are slower to index than lists
Lists are mutable; tuples are not
questions.why: Tuples cannot be changed after creation, so they can be dict keys (if elements are hashable) and signal fixed records.

questions.q: What does a generator function return when called?
o: A dictionary mapping step numbers to values
A lazy iterator that yields values on demand
A background thread that runs the whole body
A fully built list that is held in memory
questions.why: Calling it creates a generator object. The body runs only when iterated, so memory stays small for large streams.

questions.q: What does the `with` statement guarantee?
o: The block runs inside a newly created thread
The block is automatically retried on failure
Variables created inside become global names
Exit code runs, even if an exception occurs
questions.why: `__exit__` is always called, so resources like files and locks are released even if the block raises.

questions.q: What is a decorator?
o: A comment that documents a function's parameters
A class attribute that is shared between all instances
A type hint that marks a method as read-only
A callable that wraps another callable to change its behaviour
questions.why: `@dec` above a function means `f = dec(f)`. Typical uses are caching, timing, retry and access control.

questions.q: In Python, how does `is` differ from `==`?
o: `==` compares the memory addresses of objects
`is` compares only the types of the objects
`is` checks identity; `==` checks equality
They are identical for all kinds of objects
questions.why: Two equal lists are different objects, so `a == b` can be True while `a is b` is False. Use `is` mainly for None.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b = b + [4]
print(a)
o: An error
questions.why: `b = a` makes both names point to the same list, but `b = b + [4]` creates a new list and rebinds b, so a is unchanged. With `b += [4]` or append, a would change too.

questions.q: What is the purpose of `__slots__`?
o: Makes methods private to the defining class
Fixes the attribute set, saving memory
Adds runtime type checking on attribute writes
Speeds up module imports by caching names
questions.why: Without a per-instance `__dict__`, objects use less memory and block accidental new attributes.

questions.q: What does it mean for an operation to be atomic?
o: Only reads data without ever changing it
Appears to occur entirely or not at all
Executes very quickly on modern hardware
Runs on a single CPU core only
questions.why: Atomic operations cannot be observed half-done by other threads or transactions. Database commits and compare-and-swap are examples.

questions.q: In CPython, why do CPU-bound threads not run in parallel?
o: Only one thread runs bytecode at a time (GIL)
Threads cannot share any memory in Python
The operating system forbids parallel threads
Python has no thread support in any version
questions.why: The GIL serialises bytecode execution. Use multiprocessing, or native extensions that release the GIL, for CPU parallelism. Threads are fine for I/O waits.

questions.q: What is an idempotent operation?
o: Safe to repeat with the same final effect
Is always atomic as well as repeatable
Runs in constant time on every call
Never fails under any condition
questions.why: Idempotency makes retries safe, e.g. setting a value or a PUT. It matters for network calls where a response may be lost.

questions.q: What is a race condition?
o: Outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of accesses
A CPU core runs hotter than its neighbours
A task consumes memory without ever releasing it
Two tasks wait forever on each other's locks
questions.why: If two threads read-modify-write a shared value without coordination, updates can be lost. Locks, atomics or message passing avoid it.

questions.q: What causes a deadlock?
o: Too many threads are created for the number of cores
A memory leak exhausts the heap and blocks every task
One task runs too long and starves all the others
Tasks each hold a resource while waiting for another's
questions.why: A circular wait: A holds lock 1 and wants 2, B holds 2 and wants 1. Acquire locks in a consistent order or use timeouts.

questions.q: When are threads or async preferable to multiple processes in Python?
o: Compressing large data blocks in pure Python
Matrix multiplication written in pure Python
Heavy numeric loops written in pure Python
I/O-bound work waiting on network or disk
questions.why: While one thread waits on I/O it releases the GIL. For CPU-bound pure Python, processes avoid the GIL.

questions.q: What is dependency injection?
o: Import modules lazily at runtime to speed up start
Pass collaborators in rather than creating them inside
Create every dependency inside the class using it
Install dependencies from the package index at deploy
questions.why: Injecting dependencies decouples code and makes it easy to substitute fakes in tests.

questions.q: What is a regression test for?
o: Measure speed changes between releases
Ensure fixed bugs do not come back
Fit a regression model to the test results
Check behaviour under heavy load
questions.why: Regression tests lock in behaviour so later changes cannot silently break it.

questions.q: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?
o: Unit tests check the UI; integration tests check the compiler
Unit tests isolate one piece; integration tests check pieces together
Unit tests run in production; integration tests run on laptops
Unit tests need a live database; integration tests use mocks only
questions.why: Unit tests are fast and pinpoint failures. Integration tests catch wiring problems such as schema or protocol mismatches.

questions.q: Why prefer small, single-purpose functions?
o: They are easier to test and reuse
They use less memory at run time
They always run faster than long ones
Python itself requires that style
questions.why: The single-responsibility principle limits side effects and makes tests focused.

questions.q: What is a mock used for in testing?
o: Replace a real dependency with a controllable stand-in
Format source code automatically before commits
Speed up the test run by using more CPU cores
Generate realistic production data for load tests
questions.why: Mocks and fakes remove network, time or database dependence, keeping tests deterministic.

questions.q: What belongs in .gitignore?
o: Secrets, build output and local virtual environments
Source code that other developers need to see
Unit tests and the project README file
The requirements file that pins dependency versions
questions.why: Ignore generated or sensitive files. Secrets already committed remain in history, so rotate them.

questions.q: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
o: Merge keeps history; rebase replays commits onto a new base
Merge works on files; rebase works on whole repositories
Merge rewrites history; rebase keeps it untouched
Merge is local only; rebase pushes to the remote
questions.why: Rebase makes a linear history but rewrites commits, so avoid rebasing shared branches.

questions.q: What does chmod +x script.sh do on Linux?
o: Makes the file executable
Encrypts the file with the owner's key
Deletes the file after running it
Copies the file into the system path
questions.why: It adds execute permission, so the file can be run as a program.

questions.q: Why use a virtual environment or container for Python projects?
o: Make the Python interpreter itself run faster
Isolate dependency versions for reproducibility
Remove the need to write any tests at all
Prevent other people from reading the source
questions.why: Pinned dependencies avoid 'works on my machine' differences. Containers also pin the OS layer.

questions.q: Which HTTP method normally retrieves a resource without side effects?
o: POST
GET
DELETE
PATCH
questions.why: GET is safe and idempotent: it reads without changing server state.

questions.q: What do HTTP status 404 and 500 mean?
o: 404: not found (client); 500: server error
Both of them are HTTP redirect codes
404: server error; 500: resource not found
404: unauthorised; 500: access forbidden
questions.why: 4xx codes mean the request was at fault, 5xx mean the server failed.

questions.q: Why use pagination in an API?
o: Reduce the number of endpoints
Encrypt data
Cache everything
Limit response size and load
questions.why: Returning millions of rows at once is slow and fragile. Cursors or pages let clients fetch in chunks.

questions.q: What is the purpose of exponential backoff on retries?
o: Wait longer after each failure to relieve a struggling service
Retry on a different endpoint to bypass authentication
Retry instantly so the failure window stays short
Wait a fixed minute so servers can sync their clocks
questions.why: Spacing retries (with jitter) reduces thundering herds, and combined with idempotency keeps retries safe.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
o: Authentication decides what you may do; authorization proves who you are
Authentication is for APIs; authorization is for web pages only
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication happens after authorization in every system
questions.why: Login is authentication; checking whether your role may access a resource is authorization.

questions.q: What does a foreign key do?
o: Physically sorts the table by that column
Encrypts that column when stored on disk
Ensures a value refers to a row in another table
Makes every query on the table much faster
questions.why: It maintains referential integrity, preventing orphan rows, and can control cascading deletes.

questions.q: What defines a primary key?
o: A column that stores only text values
Any column that happens to carry an index
The first column listed in the table
Uniquely identifies each row, never null
questions.why: Primary keys are unique and non-null, and give rows a stable identity that foreign keys can reference.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of adding an index?
o: Faster reads and faster writes together
No effect on query speed or storage
Faster reads, slower writes, more storage
Slower reads and faster writes together
questions.why: Every insert, update or delete must also maintain the index, so over-indexing hurts write-heavy tables.

questions.q: Which problem does the 'read committed' isolation level prevent?
o: Dirty reads
Phantom reads
Lost updates in all cases
Deadlocks
questions.why: Read committed ensures you only read committed data. Non-repeatable and phantom reads can still occur.

questions.q: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
o: All left rows, with matches or NULLs from the right
Every combination of left and right rows
All rows from the right table only, matched or not
Only rows that match in both tables
questions.why: Left rows are kept even with no match, and right-side columns are NULL in that case.

questions.q: What is the purpose of normalization?
o: Compress stored data using dictionary encoding
Add indexes automatically to every column
Cut redundancy and update anomalies by splitting tables
Speed up every query by duplicating data across tables
questions.why: Normalization stores each fact once, avoiding inconsistent updates. The cost is more joins.

questions.q: What does ACID stand for in database transactions?
o: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
Availability, consistency, integrity, distribution
Atomicity, concurrency, indexing, durability
Accuracy, caching, isolation, distribution
questions.why: A transaction either fully commits or not (atomic), keeps rules valid (consistent), is not disturbed by others (isolated) and survives crashes (durable).

questions.q: Why use a transaction when moving money between two accounts?
o: It speeds up the query on both accounts
It encrypts the account data at rest
It removes the need for primary keys
Both updates succeed or both roll back
questions.why: Without atomicity, a failure between debit and credit leaves inconsistent data.

questions.q: What does a UNIQUE constraint enforce compared with a primary key?
o: No duplicate values; exactly one per table and NULLs are forbidden
Each value must exist in another table's key column
No duplicate values; NULLs may be allowed and a table can have several
Rows are physically sorted by that column
questions.why: A table has one primary key but may have several unique constraints. NULL handling varies by database.

questions.q: Why partition a large time-series table by time?
o: Partitioning removes the need for a primary key
Every query reads all partitions in parallel for speed
Time-range queries skip partitions, and old data drops cheaply
Partitioning encrypts older data automatically
