questions.why: Partition pruning limits scanned data, and retention becomes a partition drop instead of a massive delete.

questions.q: Why are columnar formats like Parquet good for analytics?
o: Always about 1% smaller than the same CSV
Read only needed columns and compress well
Support row-level locking natively
Are readable in any plain text editor
questions.why: Analytical queries touch few columns across many rows. Columnar layout lets engines skip the rest and compress similar values.

questions.q: What distinguishes replication from sharding?
o: Replication splits keys by range across nodes
Replication copies data; sharding splits it
They are two names for one single technique
Sharding copies all of the data to every node
questions.why: Replication gives availability and read scale. Sharding gives write and storage scale at the cost of cross-shard complexity.

questions.q: What does the CAP theorem say about a partitioned distributed system?
o: Network partitions never occur in practice
Pick consistency or availability during a partition
You can have all three at all times
Only SQL databases are affected by it
questions.why: When the network splits, a system can either refuse some requests (consistent) or answer with possibly stale data (available).

questions.q: When might a time-series database beat a general relational one?
o: Storing free-form documents and blobs
High-rate timestamped writes and range queries
Hosting web applications and APIs
Complex many-to-many joins across tables
questions.why: Time-series stores optimise append-heavy ingestion, downsampling and retention for sensor-style data.

questions.q: What is a key-value store best at?
o: Fast lookups by a known key
Complex joins
Ad-hoc analytics over many columns
Full-text relevance ranking
questions.why: Examples are Redis or DynamoDB. Access patterns must be known up front since queries by non-key fields are limited.

questions.q: A load draws 600 kW real power and 800 kvar reactive power. What is its apparent power?
o: 700 kVA

questions.q: A 1,000 kVA load has real power 600 kW. What is its power factor?
What does RMS value of an AC voltage represent?
o: The plain average over one full cycle
The value at the zero crossing point
The DC value that gives equal heating
The highest value reached in each cycle
questions.why: RMS is defined by heating effect: 230 V RMS heats a resistor like 230 V DC. Peak is √2 times higher for a sine wave, and the plain average of a sine is zero.

questions.q: A sine wave has an RMS value of 230 V. What is its peak voltage?
What is a power factor of 1.0?
o: Real and reactive power exactly equal
Current in phase with voltage
Current leading the voltage by 90 degrees
Zero real power delivered to the load
questions.why: At unity PF all apparent power is real power. Resistive loads have PF near 1.

questions.q: What produces reactive power demand in a typical industrial load?
o: Resistive heaters in process lines
Battery chargers running at unity PF
Incandescent lamps on the circuit
Inductive loads such as motors
questions.why: Inductors store energy in magnetic fields and exchange it with the grid each cycle, so current lags voltage.

questions.q: Why does a capacitor bank improve power factor of an inductive load?
o: It supplies reactive power locally
It removes harmonics of every order
It increases the real power consumed
It lowers the frequency of the voltage
questions.why: Capacitive vars cancel inductive vars at the load, so the grid delivers less reactive current and I²R losses drop.

questions.q: A three-phase 400 V (line-to-line) system carries 100 A per phase at PF 0.9. What is the real power (P = √3·V·I·PF)?
o: 36 kW
62 kW
69 kW
120 kW

questions.q: A 1 MVA three-phase converter at 400 V (line-to-line) delivers full apparent power. What is the line current?
o: 1.0 kA
2.5 kA

questions.q: Why are three-phase systems preferred for bulk power?
o: A higher DC voltage on the lines
No protection is needed on the feeders
Frequency is higher than single-phase
Smooth power and less copper per MW
questions.why: Three phases offset by 120 degrees give smooth power delivery and use conductors efficiently, with natural rotating fields for motors.

questions.q: What is a delta-wye (Dyn) transformer connection commonly used for?
o: Converts the AC supply into DC for the battery
Doubles the voltage without extra turns
Lowers the frequency seen on the secondary side
Gives a neutral and traps zero-sequence current
questions.why: The delta winding traps zero-sequence currents, and the wye secondary gives a grounded neutral for single-phase loads.

questions.q: What does total harmonic distortion (THD) measure?
o: The efficiency of a power converter
Departure of a waveform from a pure sine
The frequency drift of the grid supply
The RMS voltage expressed in per unit
questions.why: THD compares harmonic content to the fundamental. Inverters and rectifiers inject harmonics, which grid codes limit.

questions.q: Which harmonic orders are typical for a six-pulse rectifier?
o: Only the fundamental frequency
3rd, 6th, 9th and 12th
2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th
5th, 7th, 11th and 13th
questions.why: Six-pulse converters produce characteristic harmonics of order 6k ± 1.

questions.q: Why can harmonics cause overheating in transformers?
o: Extra eddy and hysteresis losses
They lower the winding resistance
They reduce the load current drawn
They raise the core flux density
questions.why: Eddy losses grow with the square of frequency, so harmonic currents heat windings and cores beyond what the RMS current suggests.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a harmonic filter?
o: Increase the fundamental frequency
Boost the voltage at the grid
Store energy for later release
Divert harmonic currents from the grid
questions.why: A tuned LC branch offers a low impedance at the harmonic frequency, diverting it from the supply.

questions.q: What is voltage unbalance in a three-phase system?
o: Voltage is below its nominal value
Phase voltages differ in size or angle
Frequency is above its nominal value
The neutral conductor is missing
questions.why: Unbalance introduces negative-sequence components that overheat motors and stress converters.

questions.q: What is a P-Q capability curve of an inverter?
o: Efficiency plotted against temperature
Charge level plotted against elapsed time
Voltage plotted against grid frequency
Allowed combinations of real and reactive power
questions.why: Limited by the apparent power rating, S² = P² + Q², so using more reactive power leaves less room for real power.

questions.q: A 1 MVA inverter is delivering 800 kW real power. What is the maximum reactive power available?
o: 200 kvar
450 kvar
600 kvar
800 kvar

questions.q: What does Q(V) droop control do?
o: Sets real power from grid frequency
Charges the battery by the price
Switches the contactor on temperature
Sets reactive power from grid voltage
questions.why: If voltage rises, the inverter absorbs reactive power, and if it falls, it injects, stabilising voltage without communication.

questions.q: What is low-voltage ride-through (LVRT)?
o: Staying online during voltage dips
Operating normally at low load
Charging only at low state of charge
Tripping at the first voltage dip
questions.why: Grid codes require generators and batteries to stay online during short faults, otherwise a local fault becomes a system-wide loss of power.

questions.q: What is rate of change of frequency (ROCOF)?
o: The grid frequency measured in hertz
The rotor speed of a generator in rpm
How fast frequency moves, in Hz/s
The number of cycles counted per minute
questions.why: Low inertia means higher ROCOF after a disturbance. ROCOF protection can trip generators that cannot ride through it.

questions.q: What is the nominal grid frequency in Europe?
o: 400 Hz
50 Hz
60 Hz
questions.why: Europe uses 50 Hz, North America 60 Hz. Rail networks use 16.7 Hz in some countries and aircraft use 400 Hz.

questions.q: What is the effect of a long, lightly loaded cable on voltage at its end?
o: Voltage can rise (Ferranti effect)
The current turns into direct current
Voltage always falls along the cable
Frequency changes along the cable
questions.why: Charging current through the line inductance raises the receiving-end voltage above the sending end.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a phase-locked loop (PLL) in a grid-following inverter?
o: Convert the DC bus into AC output
Track the grid voltage angle
Measure the individual cell voltages
Filter the harmonic currents out
questions.why: The PLL estimates phase and frequency so current can be injected in the right phase relative to grid voltage.

questions.q: Why does a PLL perform poorly on a very weak grid?
o: The grid frequency is too stable to track
The grid has far too much inertia
Injected current distorts the voltage it tracks
The DC link capacitor is oversized
questions.why: On a weak grid the injected current moves the voltage at the connection point, which feeds back into the PLL and can cause instability.

questions.q: What is the neutral conductor for in a three-phase four-wire system?
o: Stores energy exchanged between the three phases
Measures the frequency of the grid
Carries the DC component of the load current
Carries unbalanced currents, sets the reference
questions.why: With balanced loads the neutral carries almost nothing, but single-phase loads create unbalance current.

questions.q: What is transformer inrush current?
o: Large transient at energising from core saturation
Short-circuit current at the transformer terminals
Current drawn during normal full load
Current that flows when the voltage is at zero
questions.why: Residual flux plus switching-in can saturate the core, drawing several times rated current for a few cycles.

questions.q: How does a synchronous machine differ from an inverter in fault current contribution?
o: It gives several times rated current; an inverter ~1-1.5x
It gives no fault current, an inverter gives more
The inverter gives several times rated current
Both give identical fault current levels
questions.why: Power electronics have thermal limits, so fault current is small. Protection relying on large fault currents may not see inverter-based faults.

questions.q: What is meant by flicker?
o: Small repeated voltage swings that dim lights
A DC offset riding on the voltage waveform
A rapid shift in the grid frequency
A brief short circuit between two phases
questions.why: Rapid power swings from large loads or generators cause voltage variations; standards limit the flicker severity index.

questions.q: What is the difference between line-to-line and line-to-neutral voltage in a 400 V system?
o: Line-to-neutral is about 230 V (400/√3)
Line-to-neutral is 400 × √3
Line-to-neutral is also 400 V
Line-to-neutral is higher at 800 V
questions.why: 400/√3 ≈ 231 V. The 400 V figure is quoted between two phases.

questions.q: What does a tap changer do on a transformer?
o: Changes the turns ratio to set voltage
Filters harmonics from the output
Changes the frequency of the output
Converts the AC output into DC
questions.why: On-load tap changers move between winding taps under load so the secondary voltage stays within limits as the grid or load changes.

questions.q: Why is reactive power usually supplied locally rather than from distant generators?
o: Inverters cannot generate it at all
Regulation makes remote supply costlier per kvar
It travels faster over short distances
Long-distance transport wastes capacity and adds losses
questions.why: Reactive current occupies cable capacity and adds I²R losses, and voltage depends on local reactive balance.

questions.q: What does a STATCOM do?
o: Stores kilowatt-hours of energy for later use
Fast reactive power support from power electronics
Measures grid frequency at the substation
Delivers only active power into the grid
questions.why: A voltage-source converter with no energy storage can inject or absorb reactive power in milliseconds to hold voltage.

questions.q: What is the difference between active and reactive power control in a battery inverter?
o: They are one quantity measured in two ways
Reactive power charges the battery cells
Active power is DC while reactive power is AC
Active power moves energy, reactive supports voltage
questions.why: Reactive power only circulates between inverter and grid, so it uses no battery energy, yet it uses part of the inverter current rating.

questions.q: Ageing roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise (Arrhenius rule of thumb). Compared with 25 °C, how fast does a cell at 45 °C age?
o: Same rate
2× faster
4× faster
10× faster
questions.why: Two 10 °C steps double twice: 2 × 2 = 4× faster. Real activation energies vary, but it shows why cooling extends life.

questions.q: A battery completes 3 cycles of 50% depth each. How many equivalent full cycles is that?
questions.why: 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 equivalent full cycles, counting throughput relative to full capacity.

questions.q: What is cycle ageing?
o: Wear from charging and discharging
Failure from a manufacturing defect
Degradation from time alone
Loss from a software bug
questions.why: Each cycle stresses the electrodes (expansion, cracking, SEI growth), so wear scales with throughput, depth and rate.

questions.q: Which condition most speeds up SEI growth?
o: Low temperature and low SOC
High temperature and high SOC
Mid SOC at 15 °C
Low C-rate only
questions.why: SEI reactions are thermally activated and are faster when the anode potential is low, i.e. at high SOC.

questions.q: What is an ageing 'knee' in a capacity fade curve?
o: A point where voltage reaches zero
A fixed number of cycles
Where fade suddenly speeds up
A point where capacity recovers
questions.why: Fade is often gentle, then speeds up when mechanisms like plating or resistance growth take over. Warranty models try to stay before it.

questions.q: Which pair describes the two main ways a cell's performance degrades?
o: Capacity fade and resistance rise
Voltage rise and capacity growth
Mass loss and frequency drift
Size growth and current fall
questions.why: Capacity fade reduces energy; resistance growth cuts power capability and raises heat, and they can progress separately.

questions.q: What is loss of lithium inventory (LLI)?
o: Lithium added at formation
Lithium leaving the pack as gas
Lithium moving between racks
Lithium used up by side reactions
questions.why: SEI growth and plating bind lithium permanently, so fewer ions shuttle between electrodes, lowering capacity.

questions.q: What is loss of active material (LAM)?
o: Electrolyte lost to evaporation
Extra material added during use
Extra copper in the foil
Electrode that can't host lithium
questions.why: Particle cracking, dissolution or lost electrical contact removes host sites, reducing capacity and affecting rate capability.

questions.q: Why does a high charge rate at low temperature risk lithium plating?
o: Ions deposit as metal on graphite
The electrolyte boils
The separator shrinks
The cathode dissolves instantly
questions.why: Slow intercalation kinetics at low temperature make the anode surface potential drop below 0 V versus lithium, so metal forms.

questions.q: Why is lithium plating dangerous beyond capacity loss?
o: It cools the cell
It makes the cell lighter
Dendrites pierce the separator
Plating raises the cell voltage
questions.why: Plated lithium is reactive and can grow needles that cause an internal short circuit.

questions.q: What are the typical triggers of thermal runaway?
o: Normal self-discharge
Low state of charge storage
Heat, overcharge, shorts or damage
Light cycling at room temperature
questions.why: Abuse conditions raise cell temperature until exothermic reactions become self-sustaining.

questions.q: Why does thermal runaway release flammable gas?
o: The copper foil oxidises in air
Hot electrolyte and electrodes decompose
Water in the air turns into hydrogen
The metal case melts into gas
questions.why: Decomposition yields hydrogen, CO, methane, hydrocarbons and solvents, forming an explosive mixture inside an enclosure.

questions.q: Why is hydrogen from a failing cell a particular hazard in a container?
o: It is toxic even at low levels
It is heavier than air and pools low
Flammable over a very wide range
It cannot ignite in a closed room
questions.why: Hydrogen ignites between about 4 and 75% in air and rises, accumulating at the ceiling and creating a deflagration risk.

questions.q: What does a deflagration vent (explosion relief panel) do?
o: Turn off the PCS when pressure rises
Open at low pressure to relieve it
Cool the cells with outside air
Detect gas in the container
questions.why: If gas ignites, panels open at low pressure so the enclosure is not destroyed.

questions.q: What does NFPA 855 address?
o: Grid code limits on frequency response
Fire safety for stationary storage
Quality control in cell manufacturing
Charging rules for electric vehicles
questions.why: It sets fire protection, spacing, ventilation and hazard mitigation requirements for stationary storage.

questions.q: What does UL 9540A test?
o: Whether runaway propagates between cells
The COP of the cooling system
Capacity retention over many cycles
Converter efficiency at part load
questions.why: The test-method data feeds fire design: it shows what gas and heat a failure makes and whether it spreads.

questions.q: Why is water often used for BESS fire cooling?
o: It dissolves the electrolyte
It extinguishes oxygen
It reacts with lithium to make power
It absorbs heat and cools neighbours
questions.why: Burning cells cannot be starved of oxygen since they release it internally, so cooling the surrounding cells is the key.

questions.q: Why are clean-agent gas suppression systems limited for battery fires?
o: They freeze the pack and its coolant
They raise the cell voltage when sprayed
They conduct current to the racks
They can't remove enough heat
questions.why: Gas agents can knock down flames but won't remove heat, so cells can re-ignite or propagate.

questions.q: What can happen if a fire is extinguished but cells stay hot?
o: It can reignite hours later
Cells recharge themselves
The converter restarts
Voltage returns to nominal
questions.why: Stored energy remains and heat can restart runaway, so cooling and monitoring continue after the visible fire is out.

questions.q: What is the purpose of off-gas detection compared with smoke detection?
o: It estimates the SOC of the pack
It cools the container interior
It replaces the DC fuses
It warns before flames or smoke
questions.why: Gas such as hydrogen or CO appears minutes before smoke or fire, allowing shutdown and ventilation in time.

questions.q: What does an emergency stop on a BESS do?
o: Raise cell voltage
Start charging at full rate
Opens contactors, stops the PCS
Start the chillers
questions.why: It isolates the battery from the DC bus. Cells still hold energy, so the pack itself remains hazardous.

questions.q: Why does an internal short circuit in one cell worry designers?
o: Local heating that can spread
It lowers system voltage by 1%
It reduces the SOC error
It improves balancing
questions.why: Internal shorts bypass external protection, since the fuse cannot see them, so safety relies on cell quality, design and detection.

questions.q: Why can't a fuse stop an internal cell short?
o: The short stays inside, often small
Fuses work only on AC circuits
Fuses are always too fast to see it
Fuses can't carry DC current
questions.why: The short may only conduct limited current locally, producing heat without tripping external protection.

questions.q: What is the typical thermal-runaway onset trend of LFP versus NMC?
o: LFP never runs away
LFP starts lower and releases more
Later onset and less heat released
They are identical
questions.why: LFP's phosphate cathode is stable and releases little oxygen, giving lower heat output and later onset than NMC.

questions.q: What is a hazard unique to DC systems for maintenance workers?
o: Arcs persist; energy can't be switched off
There is no danger of electric shock
The voltage is always lower than on AC
The frequency changes during work
questions.why: A battery stays energised even with the grid disconnected, so lockout must isolate cells and verify absence of voltage.

questions.q: What is arc flash?
o: Explosive energy release from an arc
A slow overheating of a cable
A flash produced by a camera
A short voltage dip on the bus
questions.why: Faults in high-current DC equipment can vaporise metal, creating heat and pressure that injure workers.

questions.q: What is lockout/tagout (LOTO)?
o: A way to run the cooling pump manually
Isolate and lock energy before work
A way to log telemetry for audits
A way to balance cells during service
questions.why: Locks and tags show the equipment must not be energised while people work on it.

questions.q: What does insulation resistance monitoring protect against?
o: Leakage to earth before a second fault
Cell imbalance within the string
Load imbalance between phases
Poor cooling of the power stage
questions.why: Resistance dropping below a threshold warns of moisture, damage or contamination before a hazardous fault.

questions.q: What is toxic gas hazard from burning lithium-ion cells?
o: Carbon monoxide only, with no other gas
Neon released from the electrolyte
Hydrogen fluoride and other irritants
Pure oxygen from the cathode
questions.why: Fluorinated electrolytes (LiPF6) form HF, so responders need protection and sites need ventilation planning.

questions.q: What is the benefit of segmenting a container into fire compartments?
o: Stops failures spreading between racks
Reduces the purchase cost of the cells
Improves the SOC accuracy of each rack
Raises the usable DC bus voltage
questions.why: Barriers, spacing and compartmented venting keep a single-rack event from taking down the whole container.

questions.q: What is meant by 'abuse tolerance' of a cell?
o: Its maximum capacity at 25 °C
Its price per kWh at purchase
Its colour coding on the label
Resisting runaway when abused
questions.why: Nail penetration, crush, overcharge and heating tests assess how the cell behaves outside normal limits.

questions.q: Why should an overcharged cell be treated as hazardous?
o: The cell loses all voltage at once
The cathode destabilises and can run away
The cell discharges immediately
The cell becomes lighter in weight
questions.why: Above the safe limit, the cathode releases oxygen and the anode may plate, so heat generation can exceed what cooling removes.

questions.q: What does rainflow counting do in battery ageing analysis?
o: Counts the grid frequency each second
Predicts day-ahead market prices
Turns messy SOC into equivalent cycles
Measures coolant flow through the racks
questions.why: It turns irregular SOC traces into equivalent cycles with a depth, so cycle-ageing models can be applied.

questions.q: Why is a degradation model often split into calendar and cycle parts?
o: One of them is always zero
It makes the models run faster only
Different stresses, controlled separately
They are really the same thing
questions.why: Calendar ageing depends on temperature and SOC over time; cycle ageing on throughput, DoD and C-rate. Dispatch can influence both.

questions.q: What is state of power (SOP)?
o: Power it can give or take now
The cell capacity at rated conditions
The charge left in the pack
The time to reach full charge
questions.why: It depends on SOC, temperature and resistance, and limits the allowed power at each moment.

questions.q: How can SOH be measured directly in the field?
o: Measuring grid frequency
Checking the container colour
Counting alarms
A controlled full capacity test
questions.why: A reference cycle compares delivered Ah or Wh to the nameplate. Online estimators use partial data to approximate it.

questions.q: What is remaining useful life (RUL)?
o: The present state of charge
Time left until the end-of-life limit
The price of the warranty
The age since installation in years
questions.why: RUL forecasts when SOH reaches its limit using the degradation trend, and informs augmentation and warranty planning.

questions.q: Why does a hot spot in a pack matter for ageing?
o: Hot spots increase capacity
Hot cells charge slower
The hottest cell ages fastest
Temperature doesn't matter
questions.why: A temperature gradient creates uneven ageing, so cells drift apart and the pack is limited by its weakest member.

questions.q: What is second-life use of batteries?
o: Reuse in a less demanding job
Recharging a dead cell with AC
Refilling electrolyte
Replacing the BMS firmware
questions.why: Cells at 70-80% capacity can serve stationary storage, but testing, safety and economics must be considered.

questions.q: What is a key challenge in recycling lithium-ion batteries?
o: Increasing voltage
Finding enough lithium to dump
Safe, affordable metal recovery
Making cells lighter
questions.why: Collection, discharge, sorting by chemistry and recovery of cobalt, nickel and lithium are all required, with LFP being less valuable.

questions.q: Why do cell-to-cell variations matter for ageing in large strings?
o: They shrink with time on their own
They cancel at random across a string
Weaker cells age faster, so gaps grow
They only matter at the factory stage
questions.why: A cell slightly hotter or lower capacity cycles deeper, ages faster, and the spread widens, limiting usable string capacity.

questions.q: What does a rise in a cell's temperature at a constant current indicate?
o: Rising resistance or poor cooling
A shorter cycle time per day
A lower voltage drop under load
A rising capacity over time
questions.why: Heat is I²R, so extra heat points to higher resistance or reduced heat removal, and trends help spot problems early.

questions.q: Why do storage sites keep cells below a maximum temperature?
o: Heat reduces resistance permanently
Heat improves cycle life
Heat increases capacity
Heat speeds ageing and raises risk
questions.why: Temperature limits protect both life and safety, with derating applied as cells approach their limit.

questions.q: What is meant by cell swelling?
o: A rise in the cell voltage at rest
An increase in the cell capacity
Gas or expansion deforming the cell
A drop in the internal resistance
questions.why: Gas from side reactions or electrode expansion deforms cells, an early warning of ageing or abuse.

questions.q: Why is cold-weather charging restricted in BMS limits?
o: To reduce the converter size
To avoid lithium plating
To speed up balancing
To save energy
questions.why: Charge current is derated, or heating is applied, below roughly 0 to 10 °C depending on the chemistry.

questions.q: A rack holds 16 cells in series, each 3.2 V and 280 Ah. What is its energy?
o: 0.9 kWh
3.6 kWh
14.3 kWh
57 kWh
questions.why: Voltage 51.2 V × 280 Ah = 14,336 Wh ≈ 14.3 kWh.

questions.q: A container has 416 cells in series per string, each 3.2 V. What is the string voltage?
questions.why: 416 × 3.2 = 1,331 V, a typical 1,500 V DC system design.

questions.q: A 2 MWh battery is discharged at 1 MW. How long until empty?
o: 30 minutes
1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
questions.why: Duration = energy / power = 2 MWh / 1 MW = 2 hours.

questions.q: A 1 MW / 4 MWh system discharges at full power. What is the C-rate?
o: 1C
4C
questions.why: C-rate = power / energy = 1 / 4 = 0.25C, so a full discharge takes 4 hours.

questions.q: A 100 kWh battery discharges at 50 kW. What C-rate is that?
o: 1C
2C
questions.why: 50 kW / 100 kWh = 0.5C, so it takes 2 hours.

questions.q: What does depth of discharge (DoD) describe?
o: Share of capacity already used
The temperature rise during use
The ratio of voltage to current
The share of capacity still available
questions.why: DoD = 1 − SOC. At 80% DoD the battery has 20% charge left.

questions.q: What is the state of charge (SOC) of a battery?
o: Capacity compared with its new value
Energy lost in one full cycle
Remaining charge as a share of capacity
Voltage compared with nominal voltage
questions.why: SOC runs from 0% (empty) to 100% (full). SOH describes capacity relative to new.

questions.q: What is a battery cell's anode in a lithium-ion cell during discharge?
o: The porous plastic separator layer
The liquid that carries lithium ions
The negative electrode, usually graphite
The positive electrode, usually a metal oxide
questions.why: By convention the anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs on discharge: graphite releasing lithium ions.

questions.q: What is the role of the separator in a cell?
o: Carry electrons between electrodes
Keeps electrodes apart, passes ions
Collect current from the electrode
Store the lithium for later use
questions.why: A porous membrane prevents internal shorts yet passes lithium ions through the electrolyte.

questions.q: What carries charge between electrodes inside a lithium-ion cell?
o: Free protons moving through the anode
Lithium ions in the electrolyte
Electrons moving through the electrolyte
Hydrogen ions moving through the separator
questions.why: Ions move inside the cell while electrons travel through the external circuit, which is where the useful current flows.

questions.q: What does intercalation mean in a lithium-ion cell?
o: Electrolyte decomposing at the anode
Lithium metal plating on a surface
Ions inserting into a host lattice
Gas building up inside the can
questions.why: The graphite and cathode materials accept lithium ions between layers without changing structure much, which allows reversible cycling.

questions.q: What is the typical nominal voltage of an LFP cell?
o: About 3.2 V
About 4.2 V
About 1.2 V
About 3.7 V
questions.why: LFP cells are around 3.2 V nominal (2.5 to 3.65 V window). NMC cells are about 3.6 to 3.7 V.

questions.q: Which feature makes LFP state-of-charge estimation harder than NMC?
o: A voltage independent of the load
A voltage that rises with temperature
A very steep voltage curve
A very flat open-circuit voltage curve
questions.why: Across most of the SOC range LFP voltage changes only a few mV per percent, so voltage barely reveals SOC and estimators rely on current integration.

questions.q: What is voltage hysteresis in LFP cells?
o: Voltage rises in proportion to current
Voltage is the same at all SOC
Voltage depends only on temperature
OCV depends on the last charge direction
questions.why: At the same SOC the rested voltage after charging is higher than after discharging, adding another error source for voltage-based estimation.

questions.q: Which chemistry has the highest energy density among these?
o: LFP
Lead-acid
NMC
Flow vanadium
questions.why: Nickel-manganese-cobalt cells reach roughly 200+ Wh/kg at cell level; LFP about 150 and lead-acid about 35.

questions.q: What is a main advantage of lead-acid batteries?
o: High cycle life at deep discharge
Fast charging at 2C
Low upfront cost, mature recycling
Very high energy density
questions.why: Lead-acid is cheap and widely recycled, but has low cycle life at deep discharge and low energy density.

questions.q: What distinguishes a flow battery from a lithium-ion battery?
o: Energy in tanks, scaled apart from power
It stores energy in a solid lattice only
It uses no electrolyte
It cannot be cycled daily
questions.why: A vanadium flow cell stores energy in liquid electrolyte tanks; stack size sets power and tank size sets energy, suiting long durations.

questions.q: Why is LTO (lithium titanate) a niche chemistry?
o: Long life, but low density and high cost
It is unsafe to charge at low temperature
It cannot be charged quickly at all
High energy density and low cost
questions.why: The titanate anode avoids lithium plating and SEI growth so cycles reach tens of thousands, but the low voltage cuts energy density.

questions.q: What attracts interest in sodium-ion cells for stationary storage?
o: Higher energy density than NMC cells
Reliance on cobalt and nickel
Cheap, abundant materials; good in cold
Lower safety than lithium cells
questions.why: Sodium is plentiful and cheaper than lithium, though energy density is lower than LFP in current commercial products.

questions.q: Which cell format has a rigid metal case and rectangular shape?
o: Prismatic
Pouch
Coin
Cylindrical
questions.why: Large LFP storage cells (280 Ah and above) are mostly prismatic. Pouch cells use a soft foil wrap and cylindrical cells use a round can.

questions.q: What is a trade-off of pouch cells versus prismatic cells?
o: Lower energy density than prismatic
No swelling issues at all
Dense, but needs external compression
Higher mechanical strength
questions.why: The soft foil saves weight yet cells swell with gas and ageing, so modules must provide constrained support.

questions.q: How are cells assembled into a large battery?
o: Cells, then modules, racks, containers
Racks into cells, cells into modules
Modules into cells, cells into containers
Containers into racks, racks into cells
questions.why: The hierarchy builds voltage in series and capacity in parallel at each level.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cell balancing?
o: Increase the cell nominal voltage
Convert AC to DC
Reduce the number of cells needed
Keep cell voltages or SOC similar
questions.why: The weakest or most charged cell limits the string, so balancing equalises them to use capacity fully.

questions.q: How does passive balancing work?
o: Moves charge between cells with a converter
Bleeds high cells through resistors
Cools the highest cells
Disconnects the weakest cell
questions.why: It is simple and cheap but wastes the bled energy as heat and works slowly.

questions.q: How does active balancing differ from passive balancing?
o: It burns excess charge in resistors
It disconnects the highest cells
Moves charge from high to low cells
It lowers the pack voltage
questions.why: Capacitors, inductors or converters shuttle energy between cells, saving energy and balancing faster at higher cost and complexity.

questions.q: Why does the weakest cell limit usable capacity of a series string?
o: Cells share their capacity equally in series
Any one cell hitting its lower limit stops it
Each cell is charged independently of others
Current drops in the strongest cell
questions.why: In series the same current flows through every cell, so the lowest-capacity cell is full first on charge and empty first on discharge.

questions.q: What is a CC-CV charge?
o: Constant power until the pack is full
Constant voltage first, then constant current
Pulsed current at fixed frequency
Constant current, then constant voltage
questions.why: Current is held until the cell reaches its maximum voltage, then the voltage is held while current tapers down.

questions.q: Why does LFP charging often show a short taper phase?
o: Its resistance is zero near full
Flat voltage stays in CC until nearly full
Its capacity rises near full charge
It cannot charge at constant current
questions.why: Because voltage stays flat then rises steeply at the end, LFP hits its voltage limit late and spends little time in constant voltage.

questions.q: What does coulombic efficiency measure?
o: Energy stored divided by heat produced
Charge extracted divided by charge put in
Voltage at rest divided by load
Cycles completed divided by cycles specified
questions.why: A value of 99.9% means 0.1% of charge was lost to side reactions each cycle, which gradually consumes lithium inventory.

questions.q: Why is energy efficiency lower than coulombic efficiency?
o: Charge is destroyed during every cycle
Charge/discharge voltages differ, losing energy
Current direction changes the cell capacity
Cells gain voltage during discharge
questions.why: Charging occurs at a higher voltage than discharging, so each coulomb carries less energy out than it took in.

questions.q: How does internal resistance change as a cell ages?
o: It rises, cutting power and adding heat
It drops to zero at end of life
It decreases, which raises power capability
It stays constant for the whole life
questions.why: SEI growth and contact loss increase resistance, so the same current produces more heat and voltage sag.

questions.q: What is peak power capability limited by?
o: Voltage, current and temperature limits
Capacity alone at a given moment
The age of the BMS firmware
The colour of the casing
questions.why: At a given SOC and temperature, the maximum current is limited by hitting the cell voltage limits through its internal resistance.

questions.q: What is meant by nominal capacity?
o: The capacity at any temperature
The capacity at end of life
The capacity at zero voltage
Rated capacity under standard tests
questions.why: Nameplate capacity is measured at a defined rate and temperature. Real usable capacity differs with load and age.

questions.q: What is usable energy versus nominal energy of a BESS?
o: Usable equals the energy of one cell
Energy allowed within the SOC window
Usable is the energy lost in cooling
Usable is always larger than nominal
questions.why: Operators leave margin at both ends to protect cells, so usable energy is below nameplate.

questions.q: Why does the DC energy of a container differ from its AC energy at the grid?
o: Conversion and auxiliary losses in between
Cells create energy while discharging
DC and AC energy are always equal
The grid adds energy during delivery
questions.why: AC-side energy is DC energy minus PCS, transformer, cabling and auxiliary consumption, so contracts need a clear measurement point.

questions.q: What is battery augmentation?
o: Cooling the pack more strongly
Adding capacity to offset fading
Raising the cell voltage
Replacing the converter
questions.why: Operators add modules or racks in later years to keep contracted usable energy as the existing cells fade.

questions.q: What is the common end-of-life threshold for BESS capacity?
o: About 10% of initial capacity
Zero capacity left in the cell
Roughly 70 to 80% of initial capacity
About 99% of initial capacity
questions.why: Warranties usually guarantee a retained capacity in that range after a set number of cycles or years.

questions.q: What does cycle life describe?
o: How much energy one cycle stores
How many cells fit in a rack
How fast one cycle completes
Cycles before capacity hits a set limit
questions.why: For example, 6,000 cycles to 70% at 25 °C and 0.5C. Cycle life depends strongly on DoD and temperature.

questions.q: How does a shallower depth of discharge usually affect cycle life?
o: It increases the available cycles
It reduces the number of cycles
It has no influence
It changes the nominal voltage
questions.why: Lower stress per cycle slows degradation, so the total energy throughput can be larger at shallower cycling.

questions.q: What is energy throughput?
o: Energy stored in the cells at one time
Energy lost in the cooling plant
Total energy delivered over its life
Peak power in a single hour
questions.why: Warranties are often stated in MWh per MWh of capacity. It links cycles and DoD into one lifetime budget.

questions.q: What forms on the graphite anode during the first cycles?
o: A solid electrolyte interphase layer
A copper oxide film on the foil
A layer of metallic lithium
A layer of liquid electrolyte
questions.why: SEI forms from electrolyte decomposition and protects the anode afterwards, but consumes some lithium during formation.

questions.q: Why is the SEI both useful and harmful?
o: It conducts electrons through the cell
It protects, but consumes lithium as it grows
It lowers the cell voltage
It dissolves the cathode material slowly
questions.why: A stable SEI blocks further electrolyte reduction, but ongoing growth permanently removes cyclable lithium and adds resistance.

questions.q: What happens to a lithium-ion cell's voltage as it discharges?
o: It rises as the cell empties
It oscillates with the temperature
It stays fixed at the nominal value
It falls gradually, steeply near empty
questions.why: The OCV curve slopes downward with SOC, and the knee near empty is steep, which is why low-voltage cutoffs matter.

questions.q: What is the Peukert effect?
o: Delivered capacity rises at high rates
Terminal voltage rises at high rates
Capacity falls at high rates, esp. lead-acid
Cell temperature falls at high rates
questions.why: At high current the usable capacity of lead-acid drops. Lithium-ion shows a much weaker rate dependence.

questions.q: What is battery self-discharge?
o: A BMS balancing action
Faster discharge at high temperature only
Slow loss of charge while idle
Charge gained at rest
questions.why: Internal side reactions drain charge slowly even with no load. Lithium-ion self-discharge is low, a few percent per month.

questions.q: Why does a rested cell voltage differ from its voltage under load?
o: The cell recharges itself during rest
Resistance and polarisation drops that relax
Temperature falls at rest
Capacity changes at rest
questions.why: Under current the terminal voltage includes I·R and diffusion effects. After rest these relax, leaving the open-circuit voltage.

questions.q: What is the typical charge voltage limit for an LFP cell?
o: About 3.65 V
About 4.2 V
About 5.0 V
About 2.5 V
questions.why: Charging LFP above roughly 3.65 V risks electrolyte degradation, while 4.2 V is the limit for many NMC cells.

questions.q: What is the usual lower voltage limit for an LFP cell?
o: About 4.2 V
About 3.65 V
About 2.5 V
About 0 V
questions.why: Over-discharge below the limit can dissolve the copper collector and permanently damage the cell.

questions.q: Why does over-discharge damage a cell?
o: Lithium becomes more stable
The electrolyte turns into gas immediately
Copper dissolves, then re-plates as shorts
The separator turns liquid
questions.why: At very low voltage the anode potential rises until the copper foil dissolves, and the copper redeposits as metal bridges on recharge.

questions.q: What does a battery's energy density in Wh/L matter for?
o: Cell chemistry colour
Space needed per container
Cooling water flow
Grid frequency response
questions.why: Volumetric density sets how many MWh fit in a standard container, influencing land and transport cost.

questions.q: What does specific energy in Wh/kg influence?
o: The grid frequency
The thermal conductivity of the coolant
The voltage of the converter
Weight and supporting structure
questions.why: Mass matters for transport and foundations, and is key for vehicles, less so for stationary systems.

questions.q: What is thermal propagation in a pack?
o: Electricity moving between racks
Voltage moving to the DC link
Heat moving to the coolant
Heat spreading to neighbouring cells
questions.why: Pack design uses spacing, barriers and venting to stop a single cell failure becoming a rack-wide event.

questions.q: What does the BMS do if cell voltage exceeds its upper limit during charging?
o: Cuts charging, may open contactors
Raises the charge current to finish
Disables the voltage sensors
Switches off the cooling system
questions.why: Protection limits come in tiers: warn, derate, then trip, protecting cells from overcharge.

questions.q: What are the tiers of battery protection limits?
o: Warning, derating and trip thresholds
Only a temperature trip exists
One single shutdown threshold
Only a lower voltage limit exists
questions.why: Operators get early warnings, power is derated as limits approach, and contactors open only at the final threshold.

questions.q: Why is round-trip efficiency of lithium-ion lower at high C-rate?
o: Capacity grows with the current drawn
Heat leaves the cell faster at high current
Resistive losses scale with current squared
Open-circuit voltage rises with current
questions.why: Losses are I²R, so doubling the current quadruples the heat. Running at lower C-rate improves efficiency.

questions.q: What is a cell's open-circuit voltage curve used for in a BMS?
o: Maps rested voltage to SOC
Measuring temperature
Predicting grid prices
Setting the converter frequency
questions.why: A look-up from rested voltage gives an SOC correction point, limiting drift from current integration.

questions.q: What is the difference between power (kW) and energy (kWh) rating of a battery?
o: Power is voltage; energy is current
They are always equal
Power is how much it stores; energy is how fast
Power is speed; energy is quantity stored
questions.why: A 100 kW / 200 kWh unit can discharge at up to 100 kW for 2 hours.

questions.q: A chiller removes 500 kW of heat and takes 125 kW of electrical power. What is its COP?
A system has COP 3.5. How much cooling does 40 kW of electrical input provide?
o: 11 kW
37 kW
140 kW
350 kW
questions.why: Cooling = COP × input = 3.5 × 40 = 140 kW.

questions.q: A chiller has COP 4 at 25 °C ambient and its heat rejection equals cooling plus compressor work. For 400 kW cooling, how much heat is rejected at the condenser?
o: 100 kW
400 kW
500 kW
questions.why: Compressor work = 400 / 4 = 100 kW. Condenser rejects 400 + 100 = 500 kW.

questions.q: What is the role of the refrigerant in a chiller?
o: Store cold for use during later peaks
Conduct current to the compressor motor
Lubricate the circulation pump bearings
Carry heat by evaporating and condensing
questions.why: Phase change absorbs a lot of heat (latent heat) at low pressure and releases it at high pressure.

questions.q: What is the saturation temperature of a refrigerant?
o: Dry-bulb temperature of the ambient air
Boiling or condensing point at a given pressure
Temperature of the oil in the compressor sump
Freezing point of the secondary coolant
questions.why: At each pressure there is one temperature where liquid and vapour coexist, which is why pressure gauges can be read as temperatures.

questions.q: Why does a higher condenser pressure reduce COP?
o: The expansion valve is forced fully open
The compressor lifts through a larger pressure ratio
The evaporator runs colder than before
Liquid refrigerant becomes lighter and thinner
questions.why: Work per kg grows with lift, while cooling per kg barely changes, so efficiency falls.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the evaporator approach temperature?
o: Condenser water flow divided by chilled flow
Ambient air minus the coolant temperature
Leaving chilled water minus evaporating refrigerant
Compressor discharge minus suction temperature
questions.why: A small approach means a large or clean evaporator, and low lift. A growing approach can signal fouling or low refrigerant charge.

questions.q: What can low refrigerant charge cause?
o: Reduced capacity and high superheat
Higher capacity with lower superheat
Lower superheat and flooded compressor
Better COP from a lighter refrigerant load
questions.why: With too little refrigerant the evaporator starves, outlet vapour is hot (high superheat) and compressors can overheat.

questions.q: What does a thermostatic expansion valve (TXV) regulate?
o: Condenser fan speed as ambient changes
Refrigerant flow, to hold a target superheat
Compressor motor current during start-up
Coolant pump speed as the load changes
questions.why: A sensing bulb detects outlet temperature and adjusts valve opening, keeping the evaporator fed without liquid carryover.

questions.q: What is a screw compressor's advantage over scroll compressors in large chillers?
o: Higher capacity and good part-load control
Quieter operation than a scroll unit
Needs no lubrication at all
Lower cost in the 1 kW size range
questions.why: Screw units cover hundreds of kW to MW and can modulate capacity with slide valves or variable speed.

questions.q: What does a variable-speed drive (VSD) on a chiller compressor do?
o: Raises COP only at 100% load
Reduces the refrigerant charge needed
Increases the ambient temperature range
Matches compressor speed to load and lift
questions.why: Speed changes capacity continuously, avoiding on-off cycling and often improving part-load efficiency.

questions.q: What is an air-cooled chiller's main limitation compared with a water-cooled chiller?
o: It has no condenser section at all
It has no compressor in its circuit
Hotter condensing in warm weather lowers efficiency
It consumes far more make-up water
questions.why: Dry-bulb temperature is higher than wet-bulb, so it works against greater lift at peak ambient.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a cooling tower?
o: Reject condenser heat to air by evaporation
Produce the chilled water for the racks
Store ice for use at peak hours
Compress refrigerant before the condenser
questions.why: A small fraction of water evaporates, cooling the rest to near wet-bulb temperature.

questions.q: What is a dry cooler?
o: A packaged chiller with its own compressor
An evaporative tower with spray nozzles
A refrigerant compressor with a heat sink
A heat exchanger rejecting heat to air with no evaporation
questions.why: It saves water and avoids hygiene issues but is limited by dry-bulb temperature, so it can't cool below ambient.

questions.q: What is the free-cooling changeover temperature?
o: Ambient at which the condenser fails
Ambient below which the compressor can stay off
Ambient at which the coolant freezes solid
Ambient at which the compressor first starts
questions.why: When ambient is sufficiently below the required coolant temperature, a dry cooler can take the whole load.

questions.q: What is chiller staging?
o: Reducing flow to the evaporator at night
Starting and stopping chillers to follow load
Cleaning the condenser on a schedule
Raising refrigerant pressure at part load
questions.why: Running fewer units at better part-load efficiency, and adding more as demand rises, saves energy.

questions.q: What does 'lead-lag' rotation of chillers achieve?
o: Raises COP of every unit at once
Lowers the ambient temperature outside
Equalises running hours between the units
Cuts the cooling load of the site
questions.why: Alternating the duty unit spreads wear and keeps standby equipment exercised.

questions.q: Why would an operator reduce chilled-water flow at part load with a variable-speed pump?
o: Increase the refrigerant charge in the loop
Raise ambient temperature around the pump
Cool the condenser more aggressively
Cut pump energy while keeping supply temperature
questions.why: Pump power falls steeply with flow, saving more than it costs in slightly lower heat transfer coefficient.

questions.q: What does a high chilled-water supply temperature setpoint risk in a BESS?
o: Less margin to the cell limit when load rises
Lower COP from the compressor
Higher refrigerant pressure at the condenser
Failure of the condenser coil fins
questions.why: A higher setpoint saves energy, but leaves less buffer for load spikes or ambient heat, so limits must be monitored.

questions.q: What is hot-gas bypass used for?
o: Hold capacity down, avoiding surge and short cycling
Add refrigerant to a circuit with low charge
Raise capacity when demand is high
Reduce discharge pressure at full load
questions.why: Diverting hot refrigerant to the evaporator loads the compressor artificially, protecting it, at the cost of efficiency.

questions.q: What can cause high compressor discharge temperature?
o: High lift, low charge or excess superheat
High evaporator water flow
Excess liquid returning to the compressor
Low ambient air at the condenser
questions.why: Heat of compression raises the temperature. Oil breakdown and trips follow if it gets too high.

questions.q: What typically follows a clogged condenser coil on an air-cooled chiller?
o: Lower power use at the same cooling load
Higher condensing pressure, lower COP, trips
Higher capacity from a hotter condenser
Lower head pressure and less power draw
questions.why: Blocked airflow cuts heat rejection, so condensing temperature rises until efficiency and capacity fall.

questions.q: Why does Coulomb counting drift over days of operation?
o: Capacity estimates are refreshed at every rest
Sensor offset and gain errors integrate over time
Temperature slowly shifts the nominal voltage
Self-discharge adds to the measured current
questions.why: Integration turns a small constant bias into a growing error, so SOC needs periodic correction from voltage or a rest-state OCV reading.

questions.q: How does a Kalman filter combine a model with measurements?
o: It averages them with fixed equal weights
It uses the model only when voltage is high
It trusts the measurement and drops the model
It weights each by its estimated uncertainty
questions.why: A high gain trusts the measurement, a low gain trusts the model. The gain follows from the covariance of the state and of the noise.

questions.q: Why is SOC estimation harder for LFP than for NMC cells?
o: LFP cells cannot be charged at constant current
The OCV curve is flat over most of the range
LFP internal resistance is far higher at rest
LFP voltage hardly depends on the temperature
questions.why: A flat curve means a small voltage error maps to a large SOC error, so voltage correction is weak in the middle range and filters rely on current integration.

questions.q: What is the effect of hysteresis in the OCV–SOC relation?
o: OCV rises steadily with cell temperature
OCV depends on the rate of the last pulse
OCV is the same for every operating history
OCV differs after charge versus discharge
questions.why: Especially in LFP and silicon-blended cells, a path-dependent offset appears, so models include a hysteresis state or switch between curves.

questions.q: What does an RC pair in an equivalent-circuit model capture?
o: Self-discharge through the separator
The instant ohmic drop across the tabs
Thermal expansion of the cell housing
Slow voltage relaxation after a current step
questions.why: Diffusion and charge-transfer effects give a time constant of seconds to minutes, which a series resistor alone cannot reproduce.

questions.q: Why is the sampling rate important for a BMS voltage measurement used in a model?
o: Voltage cannot be read while current flows
Slow sampling aliases fast dynamics into the data
Voltage only changes once per minute in service
Fast sampling removes all SOC error entirely
questions.why: The Nyquist limit applies: dynamics faster than half the sample rate fold into the signal and bias the filter innovation.

questions.q: What distinguishes SOH estimated from capacity versus from internal resistance?
o: Neither changes as a cell ages in service
They are always identical for every chemistry
Capacity tracks energy fade, resistance tracks power fade
Capacity measures power, resistance measures energy
questions.why: A cell can keep its capacity while resistance grows, which limits power and efficiency. Both are tracked for different applications.

questions.q: Why is a cell-balancing algorithm usually run near the top of charge?
o: Balancing works only in the cold
Cells can only be balanced when fully empty
Voltage can only be measured at full charge
Steeper OCV there exposes SOC differences
questions.why: On flat curves, voltage is a poor SOC proxy. At the knees near full, small SOC gaps become visible voltage gaps.

questions.q: What is the difference between passive and active balancing?
o: Passive burns excess charge as heat, active moves it between cells
Passive moves charge, active burns it in resistors
Passive balancing raises pack capacity beyond the weakest cell
Active balancing needs no electronics at all
questions.why: Passive is cheap and simple but wastes energy. Active transfers charge via capacitors, inductors or converters at higher cost.

questions.q: What does the derivative term in a PID controller respond to?
o: The size of the setpoint only
The supply voltage of the controller
The rate of change of the error
The accumulated past error
questions.why: It adds damping and anticipates overshoot, but it amplifies measurement noise, so a filter is normally applied.

questions.q: How is integral windup typically prevented?
o: Clamp the integrator when the actuator saturates
Drop the proportional term while saturated
Reset the setpoint to zero after each step
Raise the integral gain at saturation
questions.why: Back-calculation or clamping stops the integrator accumulating error the actuator cannot act on, which avoids long overshoot on recovery.

questions.q: Why are cascaded control loops common (current inside voltage inside power)?
o: It lets the outer loop ignore the current limits
All loops must share one common bandwidth
Inner loops are faster, so outer loops see them as ideal
Cascading removes the need to tune any loop
questions.why: A rule of thumb is a bandwidth ratio of about five to ten between loops, so each can be tuned separately.

questions.q: A controller's phase margin is only 10°. What would you expect?
o: Lightly damped ringing and risk of instability
A steady-state error of exactly zero
Very slow settling with no overshoot
Perfect disturbance rejection at all frequencies
questions.why: Low phase margin means the loop is close to the instability point at crossover. Designs usually target 45° to 60°.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a feed-forward term in a power controller?
o: Add measurement noise to the loop on purpose
Slow the response to setpoint changes
Replace the feedback path entirely
Act on a known disturbance before error appears
questions.why: Feed-forward uses a model or measurement of the disturbance, so feedback only has to correct the residual error.

questions.q: What does a deadband in a droop controller do?
o: Blocks the response to large frequency events
Doubles the gain for small deviations
Pins the frequency at the nominal value
Ignores small deviations to avoid constant cycling
questions.why: A deadband of e.g. ±10 mHz reduces wear and unwanted throughput, at the price of ignoring tiny deviations.

questions.q: A 100 MW battery has 5% droop on a 50 Hz grid. Frequency falls by 0.1 Hz. What power increase does it deliver?
o: 2 MW
4 MW
10 MW
20 MW

questions.q: Why do grid-forming controls need a current limit with special handling?
o: They cannot produce any current at all
Voltage sources can output huge current into a fault
They must always run at twice the rated current
Current is irrelevant for a voltage source
questions.why: A grid-forming converter holds voltage, so a short circuit would demand high current. Limiters shift to current control or virtual impedance without losing sync.

questions.q: Why can a PLL-based grid-following converter become unstable on a weak grid?
o: The PLL can no longer measure the frequency
Injected current shifts the measured voltage, so loops interact
A weak grid raises the system inertia sharply
A weak grid supplies too much fault power
questions.why: With high grid impedance the terminal voltage depends on the converter current, so a fast PLL and current loop can interact and oscillate. Grid-forming control or a slower PLL helps.

questions.q: What is the usual cause of a ramp-rate-limited setpoint at a BESS site?
o: The PCS supports only two discrete power levels
A grid code or contract limits power changes
The BMS rejects every command it receives
The cells cannot change current quickly at all
questions.why: Ramp limits protect grid stability and are applied in the plant controller as a rate limiter on the setpoint.

questions.q: How does a state machine help in battery control?
o: Allowed modes and transitions become explicit
It guarantees no fault can ever occur
It speeds up the reactions inside the cells
It removes the need for any sensor input
questions.why: States such as idle, precharge, run and fault, with guarded transitions, make behaviour predictable and easy to verify against safety requirements.

questions.q: Why do BMS limits on charge current usually depend on temperature and SOC?
o: Plating and overvoltage risk rise when cold or full
Higher SOC always allows a higher charge current
Temperature only affects the display of SOC
Limits are fixed and never vary by condition
questions.why: Tables or maps of allowed current against SOC and temperature protect the cells; the PCS and EMS must respect them.

questions.q: What does an observability check tell you before building a state estimator?
o: Whether states can be inferred from measurements
Whether the battery is safe to transport
Whether the sensors are the cheapest option
Whether the controller can reach any setpoint
questions.why: If a state does not affect the measured output, no filter can estimate it. Adding a sensor or changing the model may be needed.

questions.q: What does the innovation (residual) sequence of a Kalman filter reveal when it is not white?
o: The sensors are noise free by design
The cell is fully charged
The filter is perfectly tuned
Model or noise assumptions are wrong
questions.why: For a well-tuned filter the residuals are zero-mean and uncorrelated. Structure in them points to model error, bias or wrong covariances.

questions.q: Why use a lookup table plus interpolation for OCV(SOC) in firmware?
o: It is more accurate than any physical model
It removes temperature dependence completely
It needs no memory on the controller
It is cheap, deterministic and easy to calibrate
questions.why: Embedded targets favour fixed-cost operations. Separate tables per temperature or a correction term handle temperature effects.

questions.q: How does a digital controller's computation delay affect stability?
o: It increases the phase margin
It adds phase lag and reduces phase margin
It has no effect below the Nyquist frequency
It only changes the steady-state gain
questions.why: A delay of T adds phase lag ωT at frequency ω, which is why high-bandwidth loops need fast sampling and compensation.

questions.q: What is an anti-islanding scheme meant to detect?
o: Loss of the communication link to the cloud
A short circuit across the DC link capacitor
Overheating of the main DC contactor coil
Loss of the grid while still energising the local network
questions.why: Islanded operation endangers workers and equipment, so converters detect it via voltage and frequency windows or active injection methods.

questions.q: Why might an EMS use model predictive control (MPC) for dispatch?
o: It ignores the limits on power and SOC
It optimises over a horizon within constraints
It needs no forecast of prices or load
It is always simpler than a fixed schedule
questions.why: MPC solves a constrained optimisation each step with a forecast and applies only the first action, so it can react to updated prices or loads.

questions.q: What is the main downside of a very aggressive Kalman filter gain?
o: The filter no longer needs a starting state
The model becomes perfectly accurate
The estimate stops responding to the input
Measurement noise flows into the estimate
questions.why: High gain trusts noisy measurements too much, so the estimate jitters. Lower gain smooths noise but lags real changes.

questions.q: How is a controller commonly validated before deploying to a real battery?
o: Hardware-in-the-loop against a plant model
Check only the style of the code
Skip testing for small parameter changes
Connect it straight to the live grid
questions.why: Closed-loop simulation with a calibrated plant, then HIL with real firmware, catches interaction faults safely before field trials.

questions.q: A 12 V source drives a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor in series. What current flows?
o: 1 A
3 A
questions.why: Series resistances add: 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. I = V/R = 12/12 = 1 A.

questions.q: In that circuit (12 V, 4 Ω in series with 8 Ω), what is the voltage across the 8 Ω resistor?
o: 4 V
6 V
8 V
questions.why: I = 1 A, so V = I × R = 8 V. The other 4 V drops across the 4 Ω resistor.

questions.q: What does Kirchhoff's current law state?
o: Voltages around a closed loop add up to the supply voltage
Power equals the voltage times the current squared
Currents entering a node equal the currents leaving it
Current is proportional to the applied voltage
questions.why: KCL is conservation of charge at a node. The loop law (KVL) says voltage rises and drops around a loop sum to zero.

questions.q: What does Kirchhoff's voltage law state?
o: Voltage across a resistor equals current divided by resistance
Currents entering a node equal the currents leaving it
Total power in a loop equals the supply current
Voltage rises and drops around any closed loop sum to zero
questions.why: KVL is conservation of energy around a loop. It is the basis for voltage-divider and loop analysis.

questions.q: Two 10 kΩ resistors form a voltage divider from a 24 V supply. What is the output at the midpoint?
o: 6 V
questions.why: Equal resistors split the voltage equally: 24 × 10/(10+10) = 12 V.

questions.q: What is the Thévenin equivalent of a linear circuit seen from two terminals?
o: Two ideal voltage sources connected in parallel
An ideal current source in parallel with a capacitor
A voltage source in series with a resistance
A fixed resistor network that has no source at all
questions.why: Any linear network looks like a source V_th behind R_th. For a battery, R_th is the internal resistance, which explains the terminal voltage sag under load.

questions.q: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are in parallel, in series with a 2 Ω resistor. What is the total resistance?
o: 2 Ω
4 Ω
5 Ω
questions.why: Parallel part: 6×3/(6+3) = 2 Ω. Add the series 2 Ω: 4 Ω.

questions.q: A 230 V heater draws 10 A. What is its power?
o: 2.3 kW
23 kW

questions.q: A 1,500 V DC string carries 200 A. What power does it transmit?
o: 30 kW
300 kW
3 MW
30 MW

questions.q: A 5 kW load runs for 4 hours. How much energy does it use?
o: 1.25 kWh
9 kWh
20 kWh
200 kWh
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 5 × 4 = 20 kWh.

questions.q: What is the unit of electrical energy that appears on a utility bill?
o: Kilowatt (kW)
Kilovolt-ampere (kVA)
Kilowatt-hour (kWh)
Kiloampere-hour (kAh)
questions.why: Bills charge for energy, which is power integrated over time. kW is a rate, kVA is apparent power, and Ah measures charge.

questions.q: What happens to the resistance of copper as it warms up?
o: It becomes zero
It rises slightly
It drops sharply
It stays exactly constant
questions.why: Metals have a positive temperature coefficient (about 0.4% per K for copper), so hot cables lose a little more power.

questions.q: A copper cable has 20 mΩ resistance at 20 °C. Using 0.4% per K, about what is it at 70 °C?
o: 20 mΩ
22 mΩ
24 mΩ
40 mΩ

questions.q: A 10 mF capacitor is charged to 400 V. How much energy is stored (E = ½CV²)?
o: 4 kJ
80 kJ

questions.q: What does a DC-link capacitor do in a converter?
o: Measures the DC current flowing in the bus
Smooths ripple and supplies current pulses
Stores enough energy for hours of backup supply
Isolates the converter electrically from the grid
questions.why: It buffers the difference between switching-frequency current pulses and the steady DC bus, keeping bus voltage stable.

questions.q: A circuit has R = 2 Ω and C = 5 mF. What is its time constant τ = RC?
o: 0.1 ms
1 ms
10 ms
100 ms
questions.why: τ = 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 s = 10 ms. After one τ a charging capacitor reaches about 63% of its final voltage.

questions.q: How long does an RC circuit take to charge to about 99% of the supply voltage?
o: About half a time constant
About one time constant
About two time constants
About five time constants
questions.why: The charge curve is 1 − e^(−t/τ): 63% at 1τ, 86% at 2τ, 99.3% at 5τ.

questions.q: Why does a precharge circuit exist in a DC system with large capacitors?
o: It raises the cell voltage before charging
It measures the insulation resistance to earth
It balances the voltage across the cell string
It limits inrush current at connection
questions.why: A discharged capacitor looks like a short circuit. A precharge resistor charges the bus gently before the main contactor closes, preventing welded contacts and tripped fuses.

questions.q: What is the main function of a transformer?
o: Filter harmonic currents out of the grid supply
Store energy for later use in a magnetic field
Convert direct current into alternating current
Change AC voltage levels magnetically
questions.why: Faraday induction links two windings; the voltage ratio follows the turns ratio. It does not work on steady DC.

questions.q: A transformer has 1,000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns, with 11 kV on the primary. What is the secondary voltage?
o: 1.1 kV
11 kV
110 kV

questions.q: Why do transformers use laminated iron cores?
o: To store DC energy
To reduce eddy-current losses
To increase the winding resistance
To lower the primary voltage
questions.why: Thin insulated sheets break up eddy-current paths, cutting I²R heating in the core.

questions.q: What are no-load losses in a transformer?
o: Copper losses that grow with the load current
Losses in the connected cables and busbars
Core losses present whenever energised
Heat from the cooling fans on the transformer
questions.why: Hysteresis and eddy losses in the core depend on voltage, not load. Copper (load) losses scale with current squared.

questions.q: A cable has 0.05 Ω total resistance and carries 100 A. What is the voltage drop?
o: 5 V

questions.q: Why is voltage drop along a cable a concern for a converter at the end of a long run?
o: It lowers the resistance of the cable run
It changes the grid frequency at the converter
The converter sees a lower voltage
It raises the current limit of the protection
questions.why: The drop is I×R. It may push the converter out of its operating window, and the lost power heats the cable.

questions.q: What is the effect of doubling a conductor's cross-section on its resistance?
o: It doubles the resistance
It leaves the resistance unchanged
It quarters the resistance
It halves the resistance
questions.why: R = ρL/A, so resistance is inversely proportional to area.

questions.q: Why is aluminium sometimes chosen over copper for large cables?
o: Lower resistivity than copper for any cross-section
Lower cost and weight per unit of current capacity
It is a better magnetic conductor than copper
It never oxidises or forms surface films
questions.why: Aluminium has about 60% of copper's conductivity but is much lighter and cheaper, so a larger cross-section is used.

questions.q: What is skin effect?
o: Current flows only through the insulation layer
DC current avoids the centre of a thick wire
At high frequency, current crowds to the surface
Voltage drops mainly at the conductor surface
questions.why: Eddy currents push AC current outward, raising effective resistance. It matters for busbars and high-frequency switching currents.

questions.q: What is the purpose of earthing (grounding) an installation?
o: Filter electrical noise from the measurements
Safe fault-current path and limited touch voltage
Reduce the load current drawn by equipment
Increase the overall efficiency of the system
questions.why: A solid earth connection lets protection operate during a fault and keeps exposed metal near earth potential.

questions.q: What does an insulation monitoring device (IMD) detect in an ungrounded DC system?
o: A rise in cell temperature inside the rack
An overload on the converter output stage
A fall in insulation resistance to earth
A loss of grid frequency at the connection
questions.why: With no earth reference, a first ground fault doesn't trip anything, so an IMD watches for leakage before a second fault creates a short circuit.

questions.q: Why is a first earth fault in an IT (ungrounded) system not an immediate trip?
o: Fault current is tiny with no return loop
The earth wire is disconnected from the frame
The fuse blows silently without any indication
The converter absorbs the fault current itself
questions.why: With no intentional earth connection, a single fault only has capacitive leakage. The danger is a second fault, which forms a short circuit.

questions.q: What does a fuse do?
o: Stores energy to ride through brief overloads
Measures the current for the BMS controller
Regulates the voltage across a connected load
Melts to open the circuit on overcurrent
questions.why: The fusible element heats under overcurrent and melts, interrupting the fault. It is single use.

questions.q: What does the I²t rating of a fuse describe?
o: The number of times it can safely open
The thermal energy needed to melt it
Its steady-state continuous current rating
Its maximum operating voltage on DC
questions.why: I²t is the let-through energy during a fault. Coordinating I²t values ensures the closest fuse to the fault opens first.

questions.q: Why must a DC breaker or fuse be rated for DC voltage specifically?
o: DC has no zero crossing, so arcs persist
DC systems need a much larger transformer
DC current is always higher than AC current
DC cables have far more resistance than AC
questions.why: AC arcs extinguish at each zero crossing every half cycle. A DC arc persists unless the device forces it out with long arc chutes or magnetic blowout.

questions.q: What is a short circuit?
o: A circuit that has no load connected to it
An unintended low-resistance path
A circuit that contains a broken wire somewhere
A circuit operating below its rated voltage
questions.why: With almost no resistance, current is limited only by source impedance and can be enormous, causing heat and arcs.

questions.q: A 800 V battery with 0.04 Ω total internal and cable resistance is shorted. What is the prospective fault current (V/R)?
o: 2 kA
20 kA
questions.why: I = 800 / 0.04 = 20,000 A = 20 kA. This is why DC protection needs a high breaking capacity.

questions.q: What is a contactor used for in a BESS?
o: Convert DC to AC for the grid connection
Estimate the state of charge of the pack
Regulate the cell temperature with coolant
Connect or isolate the battery on command
questions.why: Contactors are heavy relays that connect or isolate the pack. The BMS opens them when limits are violated.

questions.q: Why might contactor contacts weld shut?
o: Because the coil voltage is always too low
Closing onto inrush or opening under load
Because the pack is fully discharged at the time
Because the cable between them is too long
questions.why: Excess current arcs and melts the contact surfaces. Precharge and rated breaking current prevent it.

questions.q: What does the unit ampere-hour (Ah) measure?
o: Energy stored in the cell
Electric charge
Power delivered by the cell
Voltage across the cell terminals
questions.why: 1 Ah = 3,600 coulombs. Energy in Wh is Ah multiplied by voltage.

questions.q: A 280 Ah cell has a nominal voltage of 3.2 V. About how much energy does it hold?
o: 0.9 Wh
90 Wh
0.9 kWh
9 kWh

questions.q: What is efficiency in an electrical device?
o: Input power minus the power drawn by the load
Heat produced divided by the elapsed time
Output voltage divided by the input current
Useful output power divided by input power
questions.why: Efficiency η = P_out / P_in. The difference is lost as heat.

questions.q: A converter takes 1,000 kW in and delivers 985 kW. What is its efficiency?
questions.why: 985 / 1,000 = 98.5%. The 15 kW difference is dissipated as heat.

questions.q: What does per-unit (pu) notation do?
o: Express values relative to a base
Describe only the power factor of a load
Remove the need for units from every calculation
Convert AC quantities into equivalent DC values
questions.why: Normalising voltage, current and impedance to bases makes transformer ratios disappear and values comparable across voltage levels.

questions.q: What is a busbar?
o: A temperature sensor mounted on the rack
A solid conductor that distributes current
A type of capacitor used on the DC bus
A holder that carries the fuse in a panel
questions.why: Busbars carry large currents with low resistance and good heat dissipation. Joints are critical because contact resistance creates hot spots.

questions.q: Why does contact resistance at a joint matter?
o: It stores extra energy in the joint itself
Local I²R heating that can cause failure
It raises the supply voltage at the load
It reduces the effective length of the cable
questions.why: A loose or oxidised joint can have milliohms of resistance. At hundreds of amps this becomes kilowatts of heat in a tiny spot.

questions.q: What is cable derating?
o: Lowering allowed current when cooling is poor
Shortening the cable to reduce its resistance
Changing the insulation colour for visibility
Raising the voltage rating of the conductor
questions.why: Bundled cables, high ambient temperature and enclosed trays all reduce the current a cable can carry without overheating.

questions.q: What is creepage distance?
o: The gap through air between two metal plates
The thickness of the transformer core laminations
The total length of a cable run in the building
Shortest path along an insulating surface
questions.why: Contamination and humidity can let current track along surfaces, so higher voltages need longer creepage paths.

questions.q: What is clearance in insulation coordination?
o: The spacing between neighbouring battery cells
Shortest distance through air between parts
The path along an insulating surface
The overall length of the cable in the cabinet
questions.why: Clearance is set to withstand the highest expected voltage (including surges) without air breakdown.

questions.q: What is a ground fault?
o: A supply voltage that is too low at the load
Live conductor touching earth unintentionally
A broken neutral wire in a three-phase feed
A full-load operating condition on the system
questions.why: Ground faults can energise metal enclosures. Protection is designed to detect them quickly.

questions.q: What is galvanic isolation?
o: No direct conductive path between two circuits
Two circuits that share a common ground wire
Connecting circuits together with thicker wire
Reducing current by adding a series resistor
questions.why: Transformers or optocouplers transfer power or signals without a conductive connection, protecting people and measurement electronics.

questions.q: What does a Rogowski coil measure?
o: AC current, with an air-core coil
Voltage across a capacitor at high frequency
DC current flowing through a resistor
Temperature of a busbar under load
questions.why: Its output is proportional to the rate of change of current, and it cannot saturate like an iron-core current transformer.

questions.q: Why can a Hall-effect sensor measure DC current?
o: It detects the voltage drop across a fuse
It counts electrons directly as they pass
It measures resistive heating in the conductor
It senses the magnetic field of the current
questions.why: A magnetic field deflects charge in a semiconductor, producing a voltage proportional to field strength, even for steady DC.

questions.q: What is a shunt resistor used for?
o: Isolating one circuit electrically from another
Storing energy for short interruptions
Reading current from the drop across a resistor
Increasing the voltage of the measurement
questions.why: V = I × R_shunt. A precise low-ohm resistor gives an accurate reading, with a trade-off between signal and power loss.

questions.q: What is the main downside of a larger shunt resistor value?
o: It makes the measured signal smaller and noisier
It lowers the sensor accuracy at low current
It reduces the voltage reading at the terminals
More heat lost in the measuring element
questions.why: Loss is I²R_shunt. A bigger value gives a bigger signal but burns more power at high current.

questions.q: What is the difference between AC and DC current?
o: DC has a fixed frequency of 50 Hz
AC alternates direction; DC flows one way
AC flows only through resistive loads
AC is always at a higher voltage than DC
questions.why: Grids use AC for easy transformation. Batteries and PV produce DC, which is why converters sit between them.

questions.q: What is meant by a battery's internal resistance causing voltage sag?
o: The battery produces voltage only at rest
The internal resistance rises with the SOC
The voltage is independent of the current
